mwg:deprioritize-background-fetches.blocker: Simultaneous requests compete for the same bandwidth, slowing the user-initiated critical ones (quote: "When a page performs multiple simultaneous network requests, they often compete for the same bandwidth.")
mwg:deprioritize-background-fetches.outcome: Low-priority requests no longer slow critical ones; unsupported browsers ignore the option and use default priority, no fallback needed (official claim)
mwg:deprioritize-background-fetches.story: The user clicks, and the data the screen needs shares the line with analytics events and background sync sent at the same time. Lowering background requests lets the browser give bandwidth to the one the user is waiting on.
mwg:deprioritize-background-fetches.unlock: Prefetch the next chapter, next page or thumbnails freely in the background without fear of slowing the user's current search or submit; 'guess the next step' interfaces like readers and photo albums get cheaper.
mwg:deprioritize-background-fetches.support: Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state.title: Use visibility-state performance entries to tell whether the page loaded in a background tab
mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state.action: Read `performance.getEntriesByType('visibility-state')`; if the first entry is `hidden` the page loaded in the background, and the first `hidden` entry's `startTime` is when it went to the background; filter such pages out of performance analytics
mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state.blocker: Reading `document.visibilityState` when the script runs is racy: a page opened in the background and foregrounded before the script finished reads `visible` and is misjudged as a foreground load (quote: "When your script finally runs, `document.visibilityState` will synchronously read as `'visible'`, and you will incorrectly assume the page was loaded in the foreground, completely missing its initial hidden state.")
mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state.outcome: Chrome/Edge's timeline keeps the full visibility history no matter when the script runs; Firefox and Safari can only fall back to `document.visibilityState`, which the guide calls "highly inaccurate" for detecting initial background state (official claim)
mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state.story: Pages opened in background tabs render late and stretch metrics like FCP, skewing the stats. Async analytics scripts often run after the user has switched back, so checking only the current state misses it. Only Chromium gets the right answer.
mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state.unlock: A self-hosted RUM can tag background-opened visits automatically and report them separately, so median load times aren't inflated by people who middle-click links into new tabs. Chromium only for now.
mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state.support: Page visibility state performance entries: Limited (Chrome 115, Edge 115; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:efficient-background-processing.title: Use contentvisibilityautostatechange to pause animations and polling while a component isn't rendered
mwg:efficient-background-processing.action: Give heavy components `content-visibility: auto` and `contain-intrinsic-size`, and listen for `contentvisibilityautostatechange`: when `event.skipped` is true stop canvas animation, WebGL rendering and high-frequency WebSocket polling, otherwise resume
mwg:efficient-background-processing.blocker: Missing: the guide only says to pause heavy work when the component isn't rendered to save system resources and battery, without saying what concretely happens if it keeps running (quote: "Pause heavy background tasks when a component is not being rendered by the browser to conserve system resources and battery life.")
mwg:efficient-background-processing.outcome: The event follows the browser's rendering lifecycle and resumes when the element enters the pre-render margin, so content is ready when it appears; in unsupported browsers the event never fires and work keeps running, roughly emulated with `IntersectionObserver` (official claim)
mwg:efficient-background-processing.story: Simulations, charts and live data panels scrolled off-screen keep computing every frame. Tied to this event, they stop when the browser decides not to render them and restart when it prepares to. Unlike `IntersectionObserver`, it maps to render timing rather than geometric visibility.
mwg:efficient-background-processing.unlock: Put many live canvases on one page (several stock charts, physics simulations, WebGL previews) with only the ones near the viewport running and the rest paused automatically, so the laptop fan stays quiet.
mwg:efficient-background-processing.support: content-visibility: Newly (2025-09-15; Chrome 108, Edge 108, Firefox 130, Safari 26); the guide lists `contentvisibilityautostatechange` under the same status

mwg:efficient-background-processing:2.title: contentvisibilityautostatechange doesn't bubble in some implementations; delegate with capture
mwg:efficient-background-processing:2.action: Attach the listener directly to the element with `content-visibility: auto`, or add `{ capture: true }` when delegating from a parent
mwg:efficient-background-processing:2.blocker: The event doesn't bubble in some browser implementations, so ordinary listeners on a parent never receive it (quote: "The `contentvisibilityautostatechange` event does not bubble in some browser implementations.")
mwg:efficient-background-processing:2.outcome: Listening directly or in the capture phase receives the event in every implementation (official claim)
mwg:efficient-background-processing:2.story: Delegating on `document` out of habit means that in some browsers the event never travels up, the pause logic never runs, and nothing reports an error.

mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions.title: Cache inactive SPA views with content-visibility: hidden so switching back needs no recomputation
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions.action: Add `content-visibility: hidden` (optionally with `position: absolute` to take no space) to inactive SPA views and remove it on switch; fall back to `display: none` via `@supports not (content-visibility: hidden)`
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions.blocker: Destroying the old view or hiding it with `display: none` both force the browser to rebuild or recompute full layout and paint when the user returns (quote: "Both approaches require the browser to recreate or recalculate the full layout and paint when the user returns to that view.")
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions.outcome: Hidden views skip layout and paint but keep their rendering state, so switching back is near-instant; unsupported browsers render all views at once unless they fall back to `display: none` (official claim)
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions.story: Switching back and forth between tabs lays out each one from scratch every time. Hiding while keeping the cache spends almost no CPU on unseen views and reuses them on return. The cost is memory; see the next line.
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions.unlock: Tools with three to five tabs (edit / preview / settings, or several dashboard pages) can switch with zero wait while keeping scroll position and expanded state, without a framework keep-alive mechanism.
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions.support: content-visibility: Newly (2025-09-15; Chrome 108, Edge 108, Firefox 130, Safari 26)

mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions:2.title: Caching every view exhausts memory; dynamic routes need an eviction strategy
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions:2.action: Cache every view only when there are few, predictable views; apps generating many reports or routes implement an eviction strategy such as LRU and destroy old views at a memory threshold
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions:2.blocker: Unconditionally caching every view eventually bloats memory badly and may crash the browser on low-end devices (quote: "Doing so will eventually cause severe memory bloat and may crash the browser on low-end devices.")
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions:2.outcome: With eviction, frequently used views stay cached and memory use is bounded (official claim)
mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions:2.story: `content-visibility: hidden` keeps all DOM, listeners and state, so each report opened adds another copy. With unbounded routes, a long session eventually blows up the tab.

mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.title: Use blocking="render" so experiment scripts finish before first paint, replacing page-hiding anti-flicker snippets
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.action: Put the experiment script in `<head>` with `async` (external) or `type="module"` (inline) plus `blocking="render"`; add `blocking="render"` to dynamically inserted variant stylesheets too; switch variants via a data attribute on `<html>`
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.blocker: The script changes the DOM after the page starts building, so users see the original then a flash to the variant; traditional anti-flicker snippets hide the whole page with `opacity: 0` until the script runs or about 4 seconds pass, sacrificing progressive rendering and allowing clicks on invisible content (quote: "This approach sacrifices progressive rendering, allows accidental clicks on invisible content, and introduces unnecessary paint cycles.")
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.outcome: Supporting browsers don't paint until the variant is applied: no opacity, no timeout, no flicker, and HTML parsing isn't blocked; Firefox ignores the attribute, so feature-detect and fall back to the anti-flicker snippet there (official claim)
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.story: A/B tools have long had to pick a harm: don't block and it flickers, block and the page is blank for seconds and can be misclicked. `blocking="render"` gives scripts the same render-blocking behavior as stylesheets, delaying paint but not parsing. Firefox still needs the old snippet.
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.unlock: Theme, font-size and locale preferences stored in localStorage can be applied by a tiny render-blocking module before first paint, with no flash of default styles. Not supported in Firefox.
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.support: blocking="render": Limited (Chrome 105, Edge 105, Safari 18.2; not Firefox)

mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing:.title: If a render-blocking script is slow or its CDN goes down, the page never paints
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing:.action: Keep only a small stub that applies the variant render-blocking (for example under 100ms execution), load tracking and analytics separately with `async`/`defer`; don't put `blocking="render"` on non-visual scripts; consider server-side splitting for performance-critical pages
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing:.blocker: Rendering waits until the script executes, so a large or slow script directly delays first paint; a third-party CDN outage could block rendering entirely, with no developer-controlled timeout (quote: "If the experiment SDK is hosted on a third-party CDN, a CDN outage could block rendering entirely.")
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing:.outcome: Shrinking what blocks to a minimal stub keeps first-paint delay under control; the CDN outage risk remains, and the guide only asks you to check the provider's uptime and monitor LCP/FCP (official claim)
mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing:.story: Put `blocking="render"` on the whole experiment SDK and the flicker is gone, but every visit waits for it to download first; when the SDK host has an outage, the whole site is blank until the browser's own timeout.

mwg:full-session-analytics.title: Replace tracking pixels in unload with fetchLater(), letting the browser send whole-visit data when the user leaves
mwg:full-session-analytics.action: Call `fetchLater()` as soon as data exists; when state changes, cancel the previous one with `AbortController` and reschedule with the full latest snapshot; the browser sends the last scheduled payload when the user leaves or closes the tab; where unsupported, use the guide's polyfill (built on `fetch` keepalive or `sendBeacon()`)
mwg:full-session-analytics.blocker: The old trick of creating an `` pixel in an `unload` listener is very unreliable (especially on mobile) and makes pages ineligible for bfcache (quote: "Older technique like creating an `` pixel in an `unload` event listener are notoriously unreliably (especially on mobile) and can negatively impact performance (by making pages ineligible for bfcache).")
mwg:full-session-analytics.outcome: Supporting browsers reliably send the latest snapshot when the user leaves; Firefox and Safari use the polyfill, which differs only in detecting departure through `visibilitychange` (official claim)
mwg:full-session-analytics.story: Session length, whole-visit CWV and error logs are only known at the very end, and the old way forced a send on unload, which often never went out on phones and also hurt back/forward caching. `fetchLater()` lets the page keep updating 'what to send when leaving' and leaves the timing to the browser.
mwg:full-session-analytics.unlock: A long-read page can keep updating 'read up to paragraph N, stayed this long', and the final state still arrives when the tab closes, without losing bfcache. Native in Chromium, polyfilled elsewhere.
mwg:full-session-analytics.support: fetchLater: Limited (Chrome 135, Edge 135; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:full-session-analytics:2.title: fetchLater() has a roughly 64KB per-origin quota; keep payloads small and wrap calls in try/catch
mwg:full-session-analytics:2.action: Keep the payload minimal and wrap `fetchLater()` calls in `try/catch` to handle quota errors; don't use a `ReadableStream` as the body
mwg:full-session-analytics:2.blocker: `fetchLater()` throws when the quota is exceeded, and a `ReadableStream` body also errors (quote: "DO NOT use a `ReadableStream` object for the request body, as that will error.")
mwg:full-session-analytics:2.outcome: With a smaller payload and the error caught, quota problems are handled by your code instead of becoming uncaught exceptions (official claim)
mwg:full-session-analytics:2.story: A beacon rescheduled every 10 seconds carries the whole data set, which keeps growing until one call exceeds the quota and throws at the `fetchLater()` call. The guide asks you to shrink the payload up front and catch the error yourself.

mwg:identify-heavy-scripts.title: Use Long Animation Frames to find the scripts costing the most time on real users' devices
mwg:identify-heavy-scripts.action: Observe `long-animation-frame` with `PerformanceObserver` (`buffered: true`), accumulate each entry's `scripts`, group by `sourceURL`, sum `duration` and rank the heaviest scripts (including third-party chat, video and analytics), then send them to an analytics service
mwg:identify-heavy-scripts.blocker: Lab data reproduces only a small subset of real usage and differs a lot from field data, making root causes of poor performance, especially slow interactions, hard to find; the JS Self-Profiling API has higher runtime overhead (quote: "field data is often very different to lab data, which only replicates a small subset of real user scenarios.")
mwg:identify-heavy-scripts.outcome: A lightweight API can name the scripts slowing frames in field data, whether one long run or many accumulated runs; only Chrome/Edge support it, but other browsers ignore it, and the guide says the issues found mostly apply to other browsers too (official claim)
mwg:identify-heavy-scripts.story: The page stutters for users but runs smoothly on the dev machine, and profiling catches nothing. LoAF makes every frame over 50ms report which scripts ran and for how long, so you can tell in production which third party is dragging.
mwg:identify-heavy-scripts.unlock: Build a 'third-party script bill' panel: how much main-thread time each external script consumes on real users' devices, to decide whether to replace a chat widget or ad SDK. Data comes from Chromium users only.
mwg:identify-heavy-scripts.support: Long animation frames performance entries: Limited (Chrome 123, Edge 123; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:identify-inp-causes.title: Use Event Timing to split INP into three parts and find which part is slow first
mwg:identify-inp-causes.action: Use `onINP()` from `web-vitals/attribution` to get the slowest interaction's `inputDelay`, `processingDuration`, `presentationDelay` and target, and send them back to analytics
mwg:identify-inp-causes.blocker: Interaction slowness depends on user actions, device and network, and lab data reproduces only a small subset of real cases, making it hard to diagnose; without splitting, it's easy to jump straight to the interaction handler (quote: "Lab data only replicates a small subset of real user scenarios so measuring the causes of slow INP in the field is essential.")
mwg:identify-inp-causes.outcome: Split into three parts, you can tell whether the problem is other code already running, this interaction's handler, or the rendering that follows; browsers without Event Timing can't measure INP (official claim)
mwg:identify-inp-causes.story: INP is bad, so the first instinct is to optimize the button's click handler, when the real culprit is another script already running before the click, or the repaint afterward. The three-way split points the direction before digging in.
mwg:identify-inp-causes.unlock: All four major browsers can report which button was slow and in which phase, so you can build a list of slow interactions ranked by target that points straight to the component to fix.
mwg:identify-inp-causes.support: Event timing performance entries: Newly (2025-12-12; Chrome 76, Edge 79, Firefox 89, Safari 26.2)

mwg:identify-inp-causes:2.title: Use LoAF to separate style recalculation from layout time instead of heavy JS Self-Profiling
mwg:identify-inp-causes:2.action: Read `forcedStyleDuration`/`forcedLayoutDuration` (forced synchronous work inside scripts) and `styleDuration`/`layoutDuration` (frame rendering phase) from LoAF and report them separately; where the split fields are missing, fall back to the combined `forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration` and `totalStyleAndLayoutDuration`
mwg:identify-inp-causes:2.blocker: A full trace with the JS Self-Profiling API is heavyweight and can itself cause performance problems (quote: "A full performance trace using the JS Self-Profiling API is a heavyweight solution that is liable to cause performance problems.")
mwg:identify-inp-causes:2.outcome: A lightweight API distinguishes expensive selectors or broad invalidation (style) from geometry work or read/write layout thrashing (layout), which have different fixes; Chrome/Edge only, usable without a fallback (official claim)
mwg:identify-inp-causes:2.story: Knowing that 'processing took long' isn't enough: style and layout are different diseases. Telling them apart used to require a full profile, but running a profiler in production slows the page itself. LoAF reports the two separately.
mwg:identify-inp-causes:2.unlock: Production slow-interaction reports can be labeled 'style recalculation' or 'forced layout' with the responsible script and function position attached, so whoever fixes it doesn't have to reproduce it locally first. Data from Chromium only.
mwg:identify-inp-causes:2.support: Long animation frames performance entries: Limited (Chrome 123, Edge 123; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance.title: Use Speculation Rules to prefetch or prerender the next page before the user clicks
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance.action: Write `prefetch`/`prerender` rules in `<script type="speculationrules">`, preferring `where` document rules that pick links with `href_matches`/`selector_matches`, with `eagerness` (`immediate`/`eager`/`moderate`/`conservative`), optionally adding a `tag` the server can read from `Sec-Speculation-Tags`
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance.blocker: Missing: the guide only says starting to load the next page before the user visits is one of the most effective ways to improve load performance, without saying what concretely goes wrong otherwise (quote: "One of the most effective ways to improve page load performance for users navigating a site is to initiate loading the next page they're about to visit *before* they visit it.")
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance.outcome: Only Chrome/Edge support it; Firefox and Safari ignore the rules and navigate as before (official claim)
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance.story: Rules let the browser fetch or render the next page ahead of time, when the user hovers a link or even right on arrival, and you can prefetch eagerly then prerender on stronger signals with moderate eagerness. It's pure progressive enhancement: unsupported browsers gain nothing.
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance.unlock: The 'next step' of an online course, documentation or multi-step form can be prerendered so the page is already there on click, giving a static site instant navigation without becoming an SPA. Chromium only for now.
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance.support: Speculation rules: Limited (Chrome 109, Edge 109; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance:2.title: Don't speculate state-changing URLs, and beware stale content on dynamic pages
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance:2.action: In document rules, use `not` to exclude URLs like `/logout` and `add-to-cart`, admin paths, and links marked `.do-not-prerender` or `rel~=nofollow`; use prerender and high eagerness cautiously on frequently changing dynamic pages
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance:2.blocker: Speculation can hit URLs that trigger state changes, and prefetched content on dynamic pages may be stale (quote: "DO NOT speculate URLs that likely trigger state changes, like `/logout` or `/add-to-cart`, and explicitly exclude them from your speculation rules if they are likely to be included in document rules.")
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance:2.outcome: With explicit exclusions, a site-wide document rule no longer touches state-changing URLs; for stale content the guide only asks for careful judgment (official claim)
mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance:2.story: A single `href_matches: "/*"` rule pulls in every same-origin link on the page, logout and add-to-cart included, so those URLs may be requested even though the user never clicked. An exclusion list is a required companion to a broad rule.

mwg:interaction-paint-timing.title: Use interaction-contentful-paint and soft-navigation to measure content that appears asynchronously after an interaction
mwg:interaction-paint-timing.action: Observe `interaction-contentful-paint` and `soft-navigation` with `PerformanceObserver` (`buffered: true`) to attribute content painted after `fetch` and SPA route LCPs back to the interaction that caused them; or use `web-vitals` v6 with `{ reportSoftNavs: true }`
mwg:interaction-paint-timing.blocker: LCP stops after the first interaction; INP only measures to the next frame, missing content rendered after `fetch()` and SPA route changes; watching URLs alone over-reports changes that aren't route changes (quote: "Just monitoring URL updates can over report URL changes that are not linked to route changes (for example, anchor link changes, multiple "redirects" for a single route change).")
mwg:interaction-paint-timing.outcome: From Chrome/Edge 151, asynchronous paints and SPA navigations can be attributed back to interactions; Firefox and Safari can only skip these observers and keep the hard-navigation measurements, so the gap remains (official claim)
mwg:interaction-paint-timing.story: The user presses Search, the button changes color immediately (INP looks great), and results appear three seconds later. SPA page changes have no LCP at all. The new entries trace causality across `fetch`, `await` and `setTimeout`, measuring from the press to the content actually appearing. Chromium only for now.
mwg:interaction-paint-timing.unlock: An SPA can rank LCP per route, or measure the real wait from 'press Search' to results appearing, to find the slowest navigations and API responses. Chromium only for now.
mwg:interaction-paint-timing.support: Interaction contentful paint performance entries: Limited (Chrome 151, Edge 151; not Firefox or Safari); Soft navigation performance entries: same

mwg:interaction-paint-timing:2.title: Match soft-navigation paints by interactionId and report duration
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:2.action: On each `soft-navigation` entry, seed LCP with `getLargestInteractionContentfulPaint()`; match later `interaction-contentful-paint` entries by `interactionId`, not `navigationId`; report `entry.duration`, not `presentationTime` directly
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:2.blocker: In apps that render before calling `history.pushState()`, early paint entries carry the previous `navigationId`, so matching by it misses them; all timestamps are measured from the original hard-navigation origin, not the soft navigation start (quote: "If the application painted content *before* updating the URL (for example, rendering a view and then calling `history.pushState()`), those early `interaction-contentful-paint` entries were emitted before the `soft-navigation` entry and still carry the *previous* `navigationId`.")
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:2.outcome: Matching by `interactionId` includes paints before the URL update and excludes later, unrelated interactions on the new route (official claim)
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:2.story: The intuition is 'same navigationId, same page', but frameworks often paint first and update the URL later, so the most important paint ends up filed under the previous page. Reporting `presentationTime` directly gives a number measured from when the whole app opened.

mwg:interaction-paint-timing:3.title: Long-lived SPAs can't rely on getEntriesByType('soft-navigation')
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:3.action: Receive `soft-navigation` entries continuously with `PerformanceObserver` instead of querying `performance.getEntriesByType('soft-navigation')` afterward
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:3.blocker: The browser buffer keeps only the first 50 soft navigation entries (quote: "DO NOT rely on `performance.getEntriesByType('soft-navigation')` to monitor long-lived single-page applications, as the browser's buffer is limited to the first 50 soft navigation entries.")
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:3.outcome: With an observer receiving entries live, navigations after the 50th are still measured (official claim)
mwg:interaction-paint-timing:3.story: Admin panels and mail clients stay open all day and quickly pass 50 navigations. Querying the timeline afterward silently drops everything after that, with no error.

mwg:interactions-in-complex-layouts.title: Use content-visibility: auto containment to keep one column's changes inside that column
mwg:interactions-in-complex-layouts.action: Add `content-visibility: auto` and `contain-intrinsic-size` to self-contained layout units like Kanban columns or data-grid regions; where unsupported, fall back to `contain: layout style paint` via `@supports not`
mwg:interactions-in-complex-layouts.blocker: In complex layouts, changing one item (dragging a card, editing a cell) triggers chained style and layout calculations that reflow the whole page, causing dropped frames and high INP (quote: "performing a minor change to a single item—such as dragging a card or editing a cell—can trigger a chain reaction of style and layout calculations that forces the browser to reflow the entire page.")
mwg:interactions-in-complex-layouts.outcome: For visible columns the browser doesn't skip rendering; the benefit comes entirely from the layout, style and paint containment the property applies, so reflow stays within that column; unsupported browsers get a similar effect with manual `contain` (official claim)
mwg:interactions-in-complex-layouts.story: Dragging a card from one column to another reflows the whole board and the drag stutters. With each column as a containment boundary, the browser knows changes inside can't affect the outside and reflows only that column.
mwg:interactions-in-complex-layouts.support: content-visibility: Newly (2025-09-15; Chrome 108, Edge 108, Firefox 130, Safari 26)

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio.title: Use loading="lazy" on <video>/<audio> to defer poster and metadata requests until near the viewport
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio.action: Add `loading="lazy"` to below-the-fold `<video>` and `<audio>`, paired with `preload="none"` (user presses play) or `preload="metadata"` (duration and first frame fill in once in view); `autoplay` also waits until near the viewport to download and play
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio.blocker: Even with `preload="metadata"` or `preload="none"`, the browser fetches the `poster` immediately, and `preload="metadata"` still issues range requests for every player on the page (quote: "Even when `preload="metadata"` or `preload="none"` is set on a `<video>`, the browser eagerly fetches its `poster` image immediately, and `preload="metadata"` still initiates range requests for media headers across every player on the page.")
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio.outcome: Supporting browsers defer poster, preload and autoplay until near the viewport; elsewhere the attribute is ignored, and with `preload="none"`/`metadata` the full file still isn't downloaded upfront, but posters and metadata are fetched immediately; fully deferring them needs your own `IntersectionObserver` (official claim)
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio.story: A tutorial page with twenty videos, all `preload="none"`, still fetches twenty posters on load. `loading="lazy"` lets media elements wait until scrolled near, like images. Chromium only for now.
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio.unlock: Course catalogs, full podcast episode lists and product demo walls packed with media can lazy-load with plain HTML, no hand-written IntersectionObserver swapping `data-src`, and the first screen isn't held back by dozens of posters. Chromium only for now.
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio.support: Lazy-loading media: Limited (Chrome 150, Edge 150; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:2.title: Lazy video needs width and height, lazy audio needs controls, or they never load
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:2.action: Always give `<video loading="lazy">` integer `width` and `height`; always add `controls` to `<audio loading="lazy">`
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:2.blocker: Audio without `controls` has no visible box, can't intersect the viewport and never loads or autoplays; video without dimensions defaults to 300×150 and may never intersect and load, or cause layout shift when it loads (quote: "an `<audio loading="lazy">` element without `controls` cannot visibly intersect the viewport and will never load or autoplay.")
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:2.outcome: With dimensions and controls, the element has a real layout box to trigger loading and doesn't push the layout around when it loads (official claim)
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:2.story: Background music as an audio element without controls plus lazy, or a video sized only through CSS, and the lazy-load check never succeeds, so the media quietly never shows up.

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:3.title: The window load event doesn't wait for lazy media
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:3.action: Don't use the `window` `load` event to detect when lazy `<video>`/`<audio>` has loaded
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:3.blocker: The `load` event considers only eager media; lazy media doesn't count even when it starts inside the viewport (quote: "The `load` event fires based only on eager-loaded media, even if a `loading="lazy"` media element is initially inside the visual viewport.")
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:3.outcome: The guide only says not to rely on `load` and doesn't say what to use instead
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:3.story: Code that waited for `load` before initializing a player or measuring layout gets the timing wrong once lazy is added, because the media may not have started fetching when `load` fires.

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:4.title: Don't put loading="lazy" on above-the-fold or LCP video
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:4.action: Omit the `loading` attribute on the hero video (it defaults to eager) and add `loading="lazy"` only to media below the fold
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:4.blocker: Adding `loading="lazy"` to above-the-fold or LCP video delays fetching both the poster and video data (quote: "DO NOT apply `loading="lazy"` to above-the-fold or Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) `<video>` elements, as it delays fetching both the `poster` image and video data.")
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:4.outcome: The above-the-fold video loads eagerly as usual, with poster and initial media downloading immediately (official claim)
mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:4.story: Adding lazy to every `<video>` at once means even the hero video, the first thing seen, waits for the browser's distance check before fetching its poster, slowing LCP.

mwg:optimize-image-priority.title: Use fetchpriority to tell the browser which image is the LCP and which hidden ones can wait
mwg:optimize-image-priority.action: Add `fetchpriority="high"` to the LCP candidate (usually the top hero image); add `fetchpriority="low"` to images technically above the fold but not initially visible (hidden carousel slides, mega-menu images)
mwg:optimize-image-priority.blocker: Browsers assign image priorities by heuristics, and the defaults may not match the page's LCP (quote: "Browsers use heuristics to assign loading priorities to images, but these defaults may not always align with your page's Largest Contentful Paint (LCP).")
mwg:optimize-image-priority.outcome: With explicit hints, critical images load faster and non-essential ones stop competing for bandwidth; unsupported browsers ignore the attribute and keep default heuristics (official claim)
mwg:optimize-image-priority.story: To the browser, the hero image, the five other carousel slides and the promo image in a menu look about equally important and queue together. Marking the one that matters and the ones merely hidden gives bandwidth to the image actually seen first.
mwg:optimize-image-priority.unlock: A homepage whose first screen holds a carousel, menu images and avatars can order downloads 'main image first, the rest later' with HTML attributes alone, without cutting the carousel to one image for LCP's sake.
mwg:optimize-image-priority.support: Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:optimize-image-priority:2.title: fetchpriority on the wrong images: too many highs, low on lazy below-the-fold images
mwg:optimize-image-priority:2.action: Give `fetchpriority="high"` to at most 1–2 critical images and never combine it with `loading="lazy"`; ordinary below-the-fold images get only `loading="lazy"`, not `fetchpriority="low"`; never lazy-load the LCP image
mwg:optimize-image-priority:2.blocker: Too many `high` images contend for the network and dilute the boost; lazy below-the-fold images also marked `low` don't load at normal priority when scrolled to (quote: "Only use `fetchpriority="high"` on at most 1-2 critical images to avoid network contention and diluting the priority boost.")
mwg:optimize-image-priority:2.outcome: Allocated by these rules, the boost concentrates on the real LCP image and scrolled-to images load at normal priority (official claim)
mwg:optimize-image-priority:2.story: The instinct with a new attribute is to mark every important image high and everything else low; the highs cancel each other out and images below the fold crawl in when scrolled to. Priority is relative and only means something when few images are boosted.

mwg:optimize-preload-priority.title: Use <link rel=preload fetchpriority="high"> so preloaded key images stop queuing at low priority
mwg:optimize-preload-priority.action: Use `<link rel="preload" as="image" fetchpriority="high">` for images the browser can't discover early but the page needs (video posters, hero images in CSS backgrounds); use `fetchpriority="low"` for preloads of secondary fonts or background video
mwg:optimize-preload-priority.blocker: Preloads inherit the resource type's default priority, which for images is low (quote: "However, preloads inherit the default priority for the resource type and for images in particular this is low.")
mwg:optimize-preload-priority.outcome: Key image preloads rank ahead of other preloads, start earlier and get more bandwidth; unsupported browsers still preload at the type's default priority (official claim)
mwg:optimize-preload-priority.story: You finally use preload to tell the browser about the hero background early, and it gets queued at low priority, losing to everything else. Adding `fetchpriority="high"` makes early discovery mean early download.
mwg:optimize-preload-priority.unlock: Landing pages whose first screen is a video or a CSS background image can get the poster or background into the first slot just like an `` hero, without changing the design for LCP's sake.
mwg:optimize-preload-priority.support: Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:optimize-preload-priority:2.title: Too many preloads compete for bandwidth, and a wrong `as` wastes the preload
mwg:optimize-preload-priority:2.action: Preload at most about 2 images and 2–3 essential fonts per page, give `fetchpriority="high"` to at most 1–2; write `as` and `type` correctly; prefer a static HTML `` over preloading key images
mwg:optimize-preload-priority:2.blocker: Too many preloads compete for bandwidth, and with an incorrect `as` the preload isn't used (quote: "DO: Limit the total number of preloads on a page to at most 2 images and 2-3 essential fonts to prevent bandwidth contention.")
mwg:optimize-preload-priority:2.outcome: Limited in number and correctly typed, preloads go only to truly critical resources and are actually used by the page (official claim)
mwg:optimize-preload-priority:2.story: Preloading everything is the same as preloading nothing: it all fights for bandwidth. With a wrong `as`, what the preload fetched can't be used by the page, so it was fetched for nothing.

mwg:optimize-script-priority.title: Use `<script fetchpriority>` so critical scripts download first and non-essential ones step aside
mwg:optimize-script-priority.action: Add `fetchpriority="high"` to critical `async`/`defer` scripts that matter for INP; add `fetchpriority="low"` to analytics, ads, below-the-fold widgets, and parser-blocking scripts at the end of the body
mwg:optimize-script-priority.blocker: Browsers assign script priority by position and `async`/`defer`, so late-body scripts compete for bandwidth with more critical resources (quote: "Use `fetchpriority="low"` on parser-blocking scripts at the end of the body to prevent them from contending for bandwidth with more critical resources.")
mwg:optimize-script-priority.outcome: Critical scripts are queued first and non-essential scripts stop competing with key images and CSS; unsupported browsers ignore the attribute and use their own scheduling (official claim)
mwg:optimize-script-priority.story: Analytics and the main app script are both `async`, so the browser can't tell which matters and fetches them together. Marking high/low lets the developer decide the order; it's progressive enhancement, so older browsers just keep their default.
mwg:optimize-script-priority.unlock: A page loaded with chat widgets, analytics, and A/B-testing scripts can get its interactive app script in first using only HTML attributes, without rewriting third-party scripts into deferred manual injection.
mwg:optimize-script-priority.support: Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:optimize-script-priority:2.title: Give `fetchpriority="high"` to too many scripts and they all compete again
mwg:optimize-script-priority:2.action: Use `fetchpriority="high"` on at most 1–2 critical scripts; don't mark every `<script>`, only change the default when it's known to be sub-optimal
mwg:optimize-script-priority:2.blocker: Marking too many scripts high causes network contention and dilutes the boost (quote: "Only use `fetchpriority="high"` on at most 1-2 critical scripts to avoid network contention and diluting the priority boost.")
mwg:optimize-script-priority:2.outcome: Used sparingly, the elevated scripts really do go first (official claim)
mwg:optimize-script-priority:2.story: Marking every script high is the same as marking none; only with a limit does priority mean anything.

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming.title: Use `<?start>`/`<?marker>` and `<template for>` to send the shell first and patch late content in the same stream
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming.action: Place processing instructions `<?marker name>` or `<?start name>…<?end>` (wrapping a loading fallback) early in the document; later in the same response stream send `<template for="name">` and the browser swaps it in. Stream critical above-the-fold UI first and use placeholders for expensive blocks like comments, ads, and related content
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming.blocker: The guide only calls this an alternative to traditional top-to-bottom linear HTML processing, without saying when linear processing goes wrong (quote: "an alternative to the traditional "top-to-bottom" linear processing of HTML")
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming.outcome: The page shell ships immediately and database-heavy blocks are patched in when ready; Firefox and Safari need `template-for-polyfill` (official claim)
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming.story: A slow block in the middle of the document used to hold up everything after it. With placeholders filled in later in the stream, order is no longer tied to document order; native support is Chromium-only for now.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming.unlock: Purely server-rendered pages (no front-end framework) can do "shell first, slow parts later": the article shows immediately while comments and related posts stream in once computed. Native support is Chromium-only.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming.support: `<template for>`: Limited (Chrome 150, Edge 150; not Firefox or Safari). HTML processing instructions: same (unsupported browsers parse `<?marker>` etc. as comments, which the polyfill still recognizes)

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2.title: Use `streamHTML()` to pipe a fetch response straight into the DOM instead of waiting for a full JSON payload
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2.action: Use the new HTML setter family (`setHTML()`, `streamHTML()`, `streamAppendHTML()`, 24 methods with Safe/Unsafe variants) and `pipeTo(el.streamHTML())` a `fetch` response so the browser renders as chunks arrive
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2.blocker: The guide only says this replaces waiting for a full JSON payload and building the DOM by hand, without saying when that goes wrong (quote: "Stream large UI transitions in SPAs using `streamHTML()` instead of waiting for a full JSON payload and manual DOM construction.")
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2.outcome: The guide says HTML setters and streaming setters are not natively supported by any major browser yet; only `html-setters-polyfill` emulates the API (official claim)
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2.story: SPA navigations wait for the whole JSON and then assemble the DOM by hand. Streaming setters would let HTML render as it arrives, but today it's only an API shape propped up by a polyfill.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2.unlock: Island-style pages whose server returns HTML fragments could stream new content into the main region piece by piece after a link click, with no JSON API or client templates. No native browser support yet.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2.support: HTML setter methods / HTML streaming setters: "not natively supported by any major browser yet."

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:3.title: Put the live region around the progress text only, not the streamed content, and don't use `role="alert"`
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:3.action: Apply live-region markup only to the container for progress text like "Loading…"; don't wrap the whole content in a live region; don't use `role="alert"` for progress
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:3.blocker: Wrapping the whole content in a live region makes screen readers read out everything patched in when streaming completes; `role="alert"` makes NVDA say "Alert" first (quote: "Do not wrap the entire content in a live region, as this will cause screen readers to announce the full "patched" content when streaming is complete, which can overwhelm screen reader users.")
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:3.outcome: Screen-reader users hear only a short progress notice instead of being flooded with the whole page (official claim)
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:3.story: Trying to tell screen-reader users the content has arrived ends up reading the entire block at once. Shrinking the live region to the progress text gives just enough notice.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:3.support: aria-live: no support data in the guide; recorded as Widely following an existing line (mwg:language-model:3)

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:4.title: Don't put the progress notice inside an `aria-busy="true"` panel
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:4.action: Set `aria-busy="true"` on the containers being updated and back to `false` when done; keep the live-region notification outside those panels
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:4.blocker: With the notification inside an `aria-busy="true"` panel, screen readers wait until all content has loaded before announcing it (quote: "Do not nest the live region-based notification inside panels with `aria-busy="true"`, as this will prevent screen readers announcing the live region until after all of the content has been loaded.")
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:4.outcome: The progress notice is announced while loading is still under way (official claim)
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:4.story: A dashboard streams in several panels slowly, but the progress notice is wrapped inside a busy panel, so by the time it can be read it no longer means anything.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:4.support: aria-busy / aria-live: no support data in the guide; recorded as Widely following existing lines

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:5.title: Don't let focus vanish when a placeholder is replaced
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:5.action: Preserve focus when replacing a placeholder that contains the active element; keep focus where it is during and after loading rather than moving it to new content (SPA navigation is the exception: move focus to the start of the new content when streaming completes)
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:5.blocker: If a placeholder contains the focused element, focus is lost when it's replaced (quote: "make sure that focus is not lost if a placeholder containing the active element is replaced.")
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:5.outcome: The user's keyboard position isn't thrown away when content is patched in (official claim)
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:5.story: A keyboard user is sitting on a link inside a placeholder; the streamed content arrives, the whole block is swapped, and focus falls back to the top of the page. Preserve focus on replacement, or keep it somewhere that won't be swapped.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:5.support: Uses plain DOM focus handling with no new feature; no support data in the guide, recorded as Widely (same treatment as :3 and :4)

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:6.title: Reserve placeholder size up front so patched content doesn't shove the layout
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:6.action: Give placeholders stable dimensions; when the final size is unknown, use skeleton screens or CSS `aspect-ratio` to reserve space
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:6.blocker: Placeholders without dimensions make the layout jump when content is patched in (quote: "Always provide stable dimensions for placeholders. If the final content size is unknown, use skeleton screens or CSS `aspect-ratio` to reserve space and prevent jarring shifts.")
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:6.outcome: With space reserved, patching no longer pushes surrounding content around (official claim)
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:6.story: Out-of-order streaming makes content arrive late, and late content without a reserved spot pushes the whole page down while the user is reading.
mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:6.support: aspect-ratio: no support data in the guide; recorded as Widely following an existing line (mwg:css-layout:2)

mwg:performance.title: Use `async`/`defer` and inline critical CSS to stop render-blocking `@import` and big scripts in the head
mwg:performance.action: Inline above-the-fold CSS in `<head>` and defer the rest; give every non-critical script `async` or `defer` (`type="module"` defers by default); split stylesheets with `<link media>`; load third-party scripts with `defer` near the end of the page
mwg:performance.blocker: `@import` in CSS creates sequential request chains that delay the CSSOM; large non-critical scripts in the head stop DOM construction until they're downloaded, parsed, and executed (quote: "This halts DOM construction until the script is downloaded, parsed, and executed.")
mwg:performance.outcome: Scripts no longer block DOM parsing and stylesheets no longer wait on each other in a chain (official claim)
mwg:performance.story: One big script in the head and one `@import` in a stylesheet keep the page on a white screen. Inline what's critical, defer the rest, and the first paint doesn't wait for unimportant things.
mwg:performance.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:2.title: Put the LCP image in the raw HTML, don't lazy-load it, and don't make JS or CSS its only source
mwg:performance:2.action: Make the LCP image appear in the raw HTML as an `` (or ``) with `fetchpriority="high"`; never add `loading="lazy"` to above-the-fold images; don't use JS loaders to render the hero
mwg:performance:2.blocker: `loading="lazy"` on the LCP image deliberately delays the fetch until layout is done; rendering the hero with JS creates an HTML→JS→execution→image request chain (quote: "This purposefully delays the fetch until layout calculation is complete, severely degrading LCP.")
mwg:performance:2.outcome: The preload scanner finds the LCP image as soon as it sees the HTML and starts downloading early (official claim)
mwg:performance:2.story: When the biggest image is hidden in JS or marked lazy, the browser has to wait for layout or for scripts to run before it knows to fetch it. Written directly in the HTML, the scanner finds it immediately.
mwg:performance:2.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:3.title: Priority is zero-sum: give too many resources high priority or preloads and they cancel out
mwg:performance:3.action: Reserve `fetchpriority="high"` for LCP images; fonts are already high priority so don't add it there; don't preload every font
mwg:performance:3.blocker: Elevating too many resources causes network contention and negates the boost; preloading all fonts starves other critical assets (quote: "Prioritization is a zero-sum mechanism. Elevating too many resources creates network contention and negates the benefit.")
mwg:performance:3.outcome: Boosting only truly critical resources keeps the boost effective (official claim)
mwg:performance:3.story: Everyone wants to be first, so everyone gets stuck together. High priority is a scarce resource; only one or two things can have it.
mwg:performance:3.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:4.title: Yield with `scheduler.yield()` so the continuation goes to the front of the queue, not the back
mwg:performance:4.action: Split JS work over 50ms and yield with `scheduler.yield()` (falling back to `setTimeout` wrapped in a Promise); move work over 250ms to a Web Worker
mwg:performance:4.blocker: Yielding only with `setTimeout(..., 0)` puts the continuation at the back of the task queue, so it can wait a long time behind other tasks (quote: "Standard `setTimeout` places continuations at the *back* of the task queue, potentially causing long delays if other tasks are pending.")
mwg:performance:4.outcome: `scheduler.yield()` puts the continuation at the front of the queue so work resumes quickly after yielding; unsupported browsers fall back to `setTimeout` and may still end up at the back (official claim)
mwg:performance:4.story: You yield so user input can cut in, but with `setTimeout` your own second half also has to queue behind everyone else. `scheduler.yield()` yields without losing your place.
mwg:performance:4.unlock: Same as mwg:break-up-long-tasks: heavy in-browser work (parsing big files, building indexes) keeps the UI scrollable and cancellable, and long jobs don't get pushed far back just because they yielded.
mwg:performance:4.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A (for this feature's support data see mwg:break-up-long-tasks)

mwg:performance:5.title: Use `contain` and `content-visibility: auto` to keep layout recalculation inside the component
mwg:performance:5.action: Use `contain: layout style paint` on isolated UI components (modals, widgets); on large, complex pages use `content-visibility: auto` on off-screen sections paired with `contain-intrinsic-size` (with `auto` and a value derived from the content)
mwg:performance:5.blocker: Internal changes in a component trigger page-wide reflows (quote: "use `contain: layout style paint` to prevent internal changes from triggering page-wide reflows.")
mwg:performance:5.outcome: Changes inside a component only recalculate that component, and off-screen sections skip layout and paint (official claim)
mwg:performance:5.story: Change one number in a widget and the whole page reflows. Declaring containment stops recalculation at the component boundary.
mwg:performance:5.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:6.title: Add `will-change` only where it's needed, not across the page
mwg:performance:6.action: Apply `will-change: transform` to a single element only when it's about to animate (e.g. on `:hover`); also don't use `content-visibility: auto` on small, simple pages
mwg:performance:6.blocker: Indiscriminately applying `will-change` to many elements eats video memory and causes GPU crashes or sluggish rendering (quote: "Indiscriminately applying `will-change: transform` to multiple elements consumes excessive VRAM, causing GPU crashes or sluggish rendering.")
mwg:performance:6.outcome: Hinting only the right element at the right moment no longer exhausts video memory (official claim)
mwg:performance:6.story: `will-change` is a hint to the browser; sprinkled over the whole page it becomes a demand to give every element its own layer. Overdone, a performance trick ends up dragging performance down.
mwg:performance:6.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:7.title: Give images and videos `width`/`height` so space is reserved before they load
mwg:performance:7.action: Set explicit `width` and `height` on `` and `
mwg:performance:7.blocker: Lazy-loaded images without dimensions cause layout shifts when they load (quote: "Failing to specify width/height on lazy loaded images causes layout shifts.")
mwg:performance:7.outcome: Known dimensions mean space is reserved up front, eliminating CLS (official claim)
mwg:performance:7.story: Before the image arrives its height is 0; when it lands it expands and pushes the text below. Write the dimensions and the space is held from the start.
mwg:performance:7.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:8.title: If you use `srcset`, write `sizes`, or phones download the desktop image
mwg:performance:8.action: Use `srcset` with `sizes` for responsive images; use `<picture>` to offer AVIF, then WebP, then JPEG
mwg:performance:8.blocker: With `srcset` but no `sizes`, the browser assumes the image fills the viewport and downloads the largest one (quote: "Without `sizes`, the browser assumes `100vw` and downloads the largest available image.")
mwg:performance:8.outcome: The browser picks a resolution matching the actual display width (official claim)
mwg:performance:8.story: You prepared several sizes, but one missing attribute means the browser still picks the biggest. Add `sizes` and phones actually get the small one.
mwg:performance:8.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:9.title: Split code with dynamic `import()` instead of one giant `app.js`
mwg:performance:9.action: Split routes and heavy UI libraries with dynamic `import()`; configure the bundler to chunk third-party vendors separately from app logic
mwg:performance:9.blocker: A single enormous `app.js` increases parse time and memory use for the initial view (quote: "DON'T ship a single, enormous `app.js` bundle: It increases parse time and memory consumption for initial views.")
mwg:performance:9.outcome: The initial view downloads and parses only the code it needs right now (official claim)
mwg:performance:9.story: With the whole app in one bundle, low-end devices choke just parsing it. Load on demand and the first screen only pays for the first screen.
mwg:performance:9.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:10.title: Service Worker caching needs per-type strategies, versioning, and limits
mwg:performance:10.action: Use CacheFirst for hashed static assets, StaleWhileRevalidate for APIs that can be slightly stale, NetworkFirst for HTML; set expiry and size limits; don't heavily cache opaque responses with CacheFirst; always bump hashes/versions when assets change
mwg:performance:10.blocker: Not updating asset hashes or versions traps users in endless cache loops; blindly caching opaque responses eats quota and fails silently (quote: "Failing to update asset hashes/versions will trap users in infinite cache loops.")
mwg:performance:10.outcome: Users get the latest shell, static assets still load instantly, and storage isn't exhausted (official claim)
mwg:performance:10.story: A Service Worker lets pages open without the network, but with the cache set up wrong users never see the new version. Choose a strategy per resource type and add versions and limits, and the cache becomes a help.
mwg:performance:10.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance:11.title: Don't use `Cache-Control: no-store` on non-sensitive pages, or you lose the bfcache
mwg:performance:11.action: Reserve `no-store` for truly private data; for pages that just need fresh content use `no-cache` or `max-age=0`
mwg:performance:11.blocker: `no-store` keeps the browser from storing the page in the back/forward cache, making perceived performance noticeably slower (quote: "This directive prevents the browser from storing the page in the **Back-Forward Cache (bfcache)**, leading to significantly slower perceived performance.")
mwg:performance:11.outcome: The page stays bfcache-eligible and comes back instantly on Back (official claim)
mwg:performance:11.story: Writing `no-store` to "always get the latest" means every Back press reloads the page. With `no-cache` the content is just as fresh and Back is just as fast.
mwg:performance:11.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.title: Use `image-set()` in `::before`/`::after` so the browser picks the format and resolution
mwg:resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.action: Put decorative icons in a pseudo-element's `content` or `background-image` using `image-set()` with AVIF/WebP/PNG at 1x/2x, ordered from most to least optimized; write a plain `url()` line first as a fallback for older browsers
mwg:resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.blocker: The guide only says this avoids extra DOM nodes for decorative icons and lets the browser pick the best image for the device, without saying when a single `url()` or extra nodes go wrong (quote: "allows you to add decorative icons or structural graphics without cluttering your HTML with extra DOM nodes.")
mwg:resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.outcome: The browser automatically picks the best format and resolution for the device; `image-set()` is Widely available (official claim)
mwg:resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.story: Small icons on icon buttons need to cover high-DPI screens and new formats; before, you'd add an `` or ship a single file. In a pseudo-element's `image-set()`, the HTML stays the same and the browser picks.
mwg:resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.support: image-set(): Widely (2023-09-18; Chrome 113, Edge 113, Firefox 89, Safari 17)

mwg:schedule-tasks-by-priority.title: Use `scheduler.postTask()` to sort work into user-blocking / user-visible / background
mwg:schedule-tasks-by-priority.action: Use `priority: 'user-blocking'` for input handling and critical rendering, the default `user-visible` for visible but non-blocking content, and `background` for analytics and prefetching; conditionally load `scheduler-polyfill` where unsupported
mwg:schedule-tasks-by-priority.blocker: The guide only says current-view work matters more than analytics or prefetching and that the browser should stay responsive to input, without saying when unprioritized work goes wrong (quote: "Completing tasks for the current view is more important than sending analytics or prefetching assets.")
mwg:schedule-tasks-by-priority.outcome: Work is scheduled by priority and the browser stays responsive to input; Safari doesn't support it and needs the polyfill to keep prioritization (official claim)
mwg:schedule-tasks-by-priority.story: Analytics, prefetching, and UI updates used to sit in one queue, first come first served. With three tiers, background work runs only when things are idle; Safari needs the polyfill.
mwg:schedule-tasks-by-priority.unlock: A notes or document editor can put typing response first, preview re-render in the middle, and search indexing and sync in the background, so typing doesn't stutter on a single main thread. Safari needs the polyfill.
mwg:schedule-tasks-by-priority.support: Scheduler API: Limited (Chrome 129, Edge 129, Firefox 142; not Safari)

mwg:migrate-web-app-origin.title: Move origins with manifest `migrate_from`/`migrate_to` instead of making users uninstall and reinstall
mwg:migrate-web-app-origin.action: Declare `migrate_from` in the new site's manifest (optionally `behavior: "force"`), authorize `allow_migration` at the old site's `/.well-known/web-app-origin-association`, and optionally add `migrate_to` to the old manifest; both origins must be same-site (same eTLD+1)
mwg:migrate-web-app-origin.blocker: Changing origin means users must manually uninstall the old app and install the new one, losing OS integration such as taskbar shortcuts and notification permissions (quote: "This process usually causes the loss of OS-level integration, such as taskbar shortcuts and notification permissions.")
mwg:migrate-web-app-origin.outcome: Supporting browsers hand over the installation (shortcuts, home-screen icons) automatically, but data and permissions don't move; Firefox and Safari don't support it, so the old site can only show a banner asking users to reinstall (official claim)
mwg:migrate-web-app-origin.story: The product changes domain and installed users have to remove and reinstall it themselves, losing shortcuts and icons. Once both sides confirm each other, the browser swaps the shell; localStorage, IndexedDB, and permissions remain tied to the old origin and must be migrated separately.
mwg:migrate-web-app-origin.unlock: A personal tools site can split `tools.example.com/foo` into its own subdomain or merge several small PWAs, and installed users follow with one "Update" click, no announcement explaining how to reinstall. Chromium-only for now, and data still has to be moved by hand.
mwg:migrate-web-app-origin.support: Web app origin migration: Limited (Chrome 149, Edge 149; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:privacy.title: Collect data at the lowest granularity: ask for an age bracket, not a birthday
mwg:privacy.action: Collect only the granularity the task needs (an age-bracket `<select>` instead of date of birth); offer guest checkout; delete data once its purpose is fulfilled; add noise to aggregate statistics (differential privacy); don't collect "just in case"
mwg:privacy.blocker: Data you collected but don't need is lost along with everything else in a breach (quote: "If you don't have the data, you can't lose it.")
mwg:privacy.outcome: The less data stored, the lower the breach risk and the higher user trust (official claim)
mwg:privacy.story: One extra field costs nothing today but becomes one more thing to answer for when something goes wrong. Collect only the level of detail the task needs, and what you never collected can't leak.
mwg:privacy.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:2.title: Keep session identifiers in `HttpOnly` cookies, not `localStorage`
mwg:privacy:2.action: Add `HttpOnly` (with `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax`) to cookies holding session IDs; don't store sensitive tokens or PII in `localStorage`
mwg:privacy:2.blocker: Tokens and PII in `localStorage` can be read by any script embedded in the page (quote: "DON'T store sensitive tokens or PII in `localStorage`, as it is accessible by any embedded script.")
mwg:privacy:2.outcome: `HttpOnly` cookies can't be accessed by other scripts (official claim)
mwg:privacy:2.story: Tokens in `localStorage` are convenient, and just as convenient for every third-party script on the page. With `HttpOnly`, scripts can't touch them.
mwg:privacy:2.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:3.title: Send `Clear-Site-Data` on logout so no data lingers in the browser
mwg:privacy:3.action: Respond with `Clear-Site-Data: "*"` when a user logs out; when clearing the cache, trigger it via a subresource rather than the main navigation page
mwg:privacy:3.blocker: After logout, data still lingers in the browser (quote: "DO use the `Clear-Site-Data` header when a user logs out to ensure no lingering data remains in the browser.")
mwg:privacy:3.outcome: No residual data remains in the browser after logout (official claim)
mwg:privacy:3.story: You logged out on a shared computer, but the cookies, storage, and cache are still there. One response header has the browser wipe them all.
mwg:privacy:3.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:4.title: Set a strict `Referrer-Policy` so URL parameters don't leak to third parties
mwg:privacy:4.blocker: Sensitive parameters in URLs leak to third parties through the Referer header (quote: "DO set a strict `Referrer-Policy` to prevent leaking sensitive URL parameters to third parties.")
mwg:privacy:4.outcome: Cross-origin requests carry only the origin, not the path or query (official claim)
mwg:privacy:4.story: The URL contains search terms and order numbers, and every third-party request carries them out. With a restricted Referer, third parties only learn which site you came from.
mwg:privacy:4.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:5.title: Rate-limit sensitive endpoints to stop bulk scraping
mwg:privacy:5.action: Implement rate limiting on sensitive endpoints such as user search and profile views
mwg:privacy:5.blocker: Sensitive endpoints get used to scrape user data in bulk (quote: "DO implement rate limiting on sensitive endpoints (e.g., user search or profile views) to prevent bulk data scraping.")
mwg:privacy:5.story: Each profile page is public on its own, but together they make a directory. Rate limiting keeps scraping from scaling.
mwg:privacy:5.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:6.title: Use façades for heavy embeds and static links for sharing, so third parties can't track first
mwg:privacy:6.action: Show a static thumbnail for YouTube/TikTok embeds and load the iframe only after a click (using `youtube-nocookie.com` where available); replace social-sharing SDKs with plain HTML links; don't load third-party scripts on checkout or health pages; audit network requests regularly with DevTools or HAR files
mwg:privacy:6.blocker: Third-party scripts and resources are a common source of privacy leaks (quote: "Third-party scripts and resources are a common source of privacy leaks.")
mwg:privacy:6.outcome: No third-party iframe loads until the user clicks; static share links don't track users (official claim)
mwg:privacy:6.story: With one video embed and a row of share buttons, visitors are logged by third parties before they click anything. Show a static stand-in first and load only once the user shows intent.
mwg:privacy:6.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:7.title: Mediate "Sign in with…" through FedCM, and partition cookies with CHIPS
mwg:privacy:7.action: Switch third-party sign-in to the Federated Credential Management API (`navigator.credentials.get({ identity })`); add `Partitioned` (CHIPS) to cookies for 1:1 embeds instead of relying on unpartitioned `SameSite=None` cookies
mwg:privacy:7.blocker: Identity providers can track which sites a user visits before the user consents (quote: "use the **Federated Credential Management API (FedCM)** to mediate "Sign-In" flows natively, preventing IdP tracking of Relying Parties prior to user consent.")
mwg:privacy:7.outcome: The browser mediates sign-in natively, so the identity provider can't see the relying party before consent (official claim)
mwg:privacy:7.story: Every site with a "Sign in with X" button tells X which sites the user visits, even if they never press it. With the browser in the middle, nothing is revealed before consent.
mwg:privacy:7.unlock: Small sites can offer "Sign in with…" without letting the identity provider learn who visited before the user clicks; embedded widgets can keep preferences in partitioned cookies without becoming cross-site trackers.
mwg:privacy:7.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:8.title: Replace fingerprinting and UA sniffing with feature detection and UA Client Hints
mwg:privacy:8.action: Detect capabilities with feature detection (`'IntersectionObserver' in window`); when device targeting is truly needed, request only the necessary fields with `navigator.userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues()`; don't fingerprint via canvas, font lists, or media-device enumeration, and don't rely on the full `navigator.userAgent`
mwg:privacy:8.blocker: Fingerprinting relies on unchanging characteristics and happens invisibly, so users can neither opt out nor clear the identifier (quote: "Fingerprinting takes away user control because it relies on unchanging characteristics and happens invisibly, preventing users from opting out or clearing their identifier.")
mwg:privacy:8.outcome: The guide only asks for feature detection and UA-CH, without saying how much UA-CH reduces fingerprinting (official claim)
mwg:privacy:8.story: Parsing the UA string or reading a canvas to judge browser capabilities quietly creates an identifier users can't delete. Ask "is this feature here?" instead, and request explicit device fields only when needed.
mwg:privacy:8.unlock: Pages that offer per-platform downloads or installers by CPU architecture can ask for just the platform version and architecture, without parsing the whole UA string or fingerprinting.
mwg:privacy:8.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:privacy:9.title: Use the `<permission>` element so permission requests are user-initiated
mwg:privacy:9.action: Where supported, request permissions declaratively with the Page Embedded Permission Control (`<permission type="geolocation">`) with a regular button inside as fallback; explain the reason and context before requesting powerful permissions like camera or location
mwg:privacy:9.blocker: The guide only asks for a clear reason and context before requesting permissions, without saying when an abrupt permission prompt goes wrong (quote: "DO provide a clear reason and context *before* requesting powerful browser permissions (e.g., camera, location).")
mwg:privacy:9.outcome: The guide only says `<permission>` makes requests declarative, user-initiated, and acts as a data mediator, without saying how much it improves any problem (official claim)
mwg:privacy:9.story: Permission dialogs often pop up before users know why. `<permission>` turns the request into an on-page control the user presses themselves; unsupported browsers just see a regular button.
mwg:privacy:9.unlock: A map or store-finder page can make "Use my location" a native in-page control, so the permission request always comes from a user click and never pops up on load.
mwg:privacy:9.support: No browser support data in the guide (only "if supported"); recorded as N/A

mwg:client-side-encryption.title: Use `encapsulateKey()` (MLKEM768-X25519) plus AEAD for post-quantum envelope encryption in the browser
mwg:client-side-encryption.action: The recipient generates a non-extractable key pair with `crypto.subtle.generateKey('MLKEM768-X25519', false, …)`, stores it in IndexedDB, and exports the public key as `'raw-public'`; for each message the sender calls `encapsulateKey()` to get a one-time shared key and ciphertext capsule, encrypts with `ChaCha20-Poly1305` or `AES-GCM`, and sends `{ capsule, iv, ciphertext }`
mwg:client-side-encryption.blocker: The guide only says the hybrid KEM keeps the shared secret secure as long as either algorithm holds, without saying when classical-only key exchange goes wrong (quote: "it combines post-quantum ML-KEM (standardized in NIST FIPS 203) with classical `'X25519'` so the shared secret remains secure as long as either algorithm holds.")
mwg:client-side-encryption.outcome: Supporting browsers can do post-quantum envelope encryption locally; without `SubtleCrypto.supports()`/`encapsulateKey()` it falls back to classical X25519 + HKDF + AES-GCM (official claim)
mwg:client-side-encryption.story: End-to-end encryption in the browser no longer needs a crypto library, and the private key never leaves its `CryptoKey`. Browsers without the new algorithms fall back to classical key exchange behind the same interface.
mwg:client-side-encryption.unlock: A diary or notes app can encrypt each entry in the browser before upload so the server only stores ciphertext, with a non-extractable `CryptoKey` and no bundled crypto library. Falls back to classical exchange where the new algorithms aren't supported.
mwg:client-side-encryption.support: Web Cryptography: Widely (2017-09-19); X25519 deriveBits: Newly (2025-02-06). The guide gives no support data for ML-KEM/`encapsulateKey()`; recorded as Newly, the lowest listed

mwg:client-side-encryption:2.title: Bind unencrypted metadata into the AEAD tag with `additionalData`
mwg:client-side-encryption:2.action: Pass unencrypted metadata such as record ID, recipient ID, or protocol version as `additionalData` when encrypting; use a fresh random 12-byte IV every time and never reuse an `(iv, key)` pair
mwg:client-side-encryption:2.blocker: Without binding, tampering with the metadata next to the ciphertext goes unnoticed (quote: "Bind unencrypted metadata (such as a record ID, recipient ID, or protocol version) to the authentication tag via `additionalData` so tampering with either the ciphertext or the metadata causes `decrypt()` to reject with `OperationError`.")
mwg:client-side-encryption:2.outcome: If either the ciphertext or the metadata is changed, `decrypt()` rejects with `OperationError` (official claim)
mwg:client-side-encryption:2.story: The ciphertext itself is authenticated, but "who it's for, which record" sits beside it, so an attacker can move ciphertext under another record. Bind the metadata into the tag and moved ciphertext won't decrypt.

mwg:client-side-encryption:3.title: New algorithms reject `'raw'`: write `'raw-public'` / `'raw-seed'` / `'raw-secret'` explicitly
mwg:client-side-encryption:3.action: Always specify an explicit format in `importKey()`/`exportKey()` for `MLKEM768-X25519`, `ML-KEM-*`, and `ChaCha20-Poly1305`; import KEM private keys with only `['decapsulateKey']`; use only the three algorithm names the guide lists
mwg:client-side-encryption:3.blocker: Sticking with the legacy `'raw'` format makes the new algorithms throw `NotSupportedError` (quote: "Modern WebCrypto algorithms (…) **reject the legacy `'raw'` format** in `importKey()` and `exportKey()` with a `NotSupportedError`.")
mwg:client-side-encryption:3.outcome: With explicit formats, import and export work; the classical fallback path still uses `'raw'` (official claim)
mwg:client-side-encryption:3.story: Writing `'raw'` out of habit makes the whole flow fail at step one on the new algorithms. The old and new paths use different format names and must be written separately.
mwg:client-side-encryption:3.support: Same as mwg:client-side-encryption; recorded as Newly

mwg:client-side-encryption:4.title: Call `SubtleCrypto.supports()` on the constructor, not on `crypto.subtle`
mwg:client-side-encryption:4.action: Detect with `globalThis.SubtleCrypto?.supports?.('encapsulateKey', 'MLKEM768-X25519', 'ChaCha20-Poly1305')`; include an `iv` when probing `'encrypt'`/`'decrypt'`
mwg:client-side-encryption:4.blocker: Looking for `supports` on `crypto.subtle` gets `undefined` (quote: "`globalThis.SubtleCrypto?.supports?.(…)` is a synchronous static method returning a boolean (`crypto.subtle.supports` is `undefined`).")
mwg:client-side-encryption:4.outcome: Detecting on the right object is what lets you choose between the post-quantum and classical paths (official claim)
mwg:client-side-encryption:4.story: With detection on the wrong object, the answer is always "unsupported", and even supporting browsers get sent down the classical path.
mwg:client-side-encryption:4.support: Same as mwg:client-side-encryption; recorded as Newly

mwg:digital-signatures.title: Sign and verify in the browser with ML-DSA, no shared secret key needed
mwg:digital-signatures.action: Generate a key pair with `crypto.subtle.generateKey('ML-DSA-65', false, ['sign', 'verify'])`, export the public key as `'raw-public'` for verifiers, and `sign()`/`verify()` messages, tokens, or release manifests; fall back to `'Ed25519'` (or `'ECDSA'` P-256) where unsupported
mwg:digital-signatures.blocker: The guide only says digital signatures guarantee integrity and signer authenticity without shared secret keys, without saying when other approaches go wrong (quote: "Digital signatures guarantee data integrity and signer authenticity without requiring shared secret keys.")
mwg:digital-signatures.outcome: Supporting browsers sign with post-quantum ML-DSA; others fall back to classical Ed25519 (official claim)
mwg:digital-signatures.story: Confirming in the browser that a manifest hasn't been altered and really came from someone used to mean shipping a crypto library or deferring to the server. Now `crypto.subtle` does it directly, with a post-quantum option.
mwg:digital-signatures.unlock: A static site can ship a signed release manifest that visitors' browsers verify after downloading files, without trusting the CDN in between; exported notes can carry a signature proving they weren't altered.
mwg:digital-signatures.support: Web Cryptography: Widely (2017-09-19); Ed25519 sign: Newly (2025-05-29). The guide gives no support data for ML-DSA; recorded as Newly, the lowest listed
