mwg:digital-signatures:2.title: Use `context` for domain separation so a signature for one purpose can't be replayed elsewhere
mwg:digital-signatures:2.action: Pass `{ name: 'ML-DSA-65', context }` (0–255 bytes, identical on both sides) to `sign()`/`verify()`; when falling back to Ed25519/ECDSA, prepend a length-prefixed context header to the data yourself
mwg:digital-signatures:2.blocker: When one key pair is shared, a signature made for one purpose can be replayed in another part of the app; classical algorithms also silently ignore a `context` property (quote: "To prevent a signature created for one purpose from being replayed in another part of your application or protocol that shares the same key pair, bind the signature to a domain-separation `context`.")
mwg:digital-signatures:2.outcome: ML-DSA binds context natively, so verification fails under a different context; the classical path needs the manual prefix for the same effect (official claim)
mwg:digital-signatures:2.story: If the same key signs both login challenges and release manifests, an attacker might pass one off as the other. Binding a purpose label keeps each signature valid only for its purpose; the classical fallback silently drops the label, so add it by hand.
mwg:digital-signatures:2.unlock: One browser-side identity key can sign login challenges, comments, and file manifests without any of those signatures being reusable for another purpose, instead of managing a key per purpose.
mwg:digital-signatures:2.support: Same as mwg:digital-signatures; recorded as Newly

mwg:digital-signatures:3.title: ML-DSA rejects `'raw'`: use `'raw-public'` for public keys and `'raw-seed'` for private keys
mwg:digital-signatures:3.action: Specify `'raw-public'`, `'raw-seed'`, `'spki'`, `'pkcs8'`, or `'jwk'` when importing/exporting ML-DSA keys; import public keys with only `['verify']` and private keys with only `['sign']`; don't use pre-standardization names like `'Dilithium'`
mwg:digital-signatures:3.blocker: Sticking with the legacy `'raw'` format makes ML-DSA throw `NotSupportedError` (quote: "`'ML-DSA-44'`, `'ML-DSA-65'`, and `'ML-DSA-87'` **reject the legacy `'raw'` format** in `importKey()` and `exportKey()` with a `NotSupportedError`.")
mwg:digital-signatures:3.outcome: With explicit formats, import and export work; the Ed25519 fallback path still uses `'raw'` (official claim)
mwg:digital-signatures:3.story: Same pitfall as mwg:client-side-encryption:3: the new algorithms renamed the formats, and writing it the old way fails at the first step.
mwg:digital-signatures:3.support: Same as mwg:digital-signatures; recorded as Newly

mwg:digital-signatures:4.title: Call `SubtleCrypto.supports()` on the constructor, not on `crypto.subtle`
mwg:digital-signatures:4.action: Detect with `globalThis.SubtleCrypto?.supports?.('sign', 'ML-DSA-65')` to choose between ML-DSA and Ed25519
mwg:digital-signatures:4.blocker: Looking for `supports` on `crypto.subtle` gets `undefined` (quote: "`globalThis.SubtleCrypto?.supports?.('sign', 'ML-DSA-65')` is a synchronous static method returning a boolean (`crypto.subtle.supports` is `undefined`).")
mwg:digital-signatures:4.outcome: Detecting on the right object is what makes the branching correct (official claim)
mwg:digital-signatures:4.story: Same as mwg:client-side-encryption:4: detection on the wrong object always takes the fallback.
mwg:digital-signatures:4.support: Same as mwg:digital-signatures; recorded as Newly

mwg:local-network-access.title: Use `targetAddressSpace` so an https page can reach http devices on the LAN
mwg:local-network-access.action: Add `targetAddressSpace: 'local'` or `'loopback'` to `fetch()`/`Request` calls to LAN devices (printers, IoT hubs, routers) or local companion apps; connect after the user grants the `local-network`/`loopback-network` permission
mwg:local-network-access.blocker: Mixed Content checks run before DNS resolution, so an https page's request to an http LAN endpoint is blocked as mixed content (quote: "Mixed Content checks run *before* DNS resolution. Declaring `targetAddressSpace: 'local'` (…) informs the browser ahead of DNS resolution that an `http://` URL (…) targets a local/loopback endpoint and should be exempted from Mixed Content blocking once the user grants the permission.")
mwg:local-network-access.outcome: Supporting browsers allow it after permission and verify after resolution that the IP really is in the declared address space (aborting otherwise); Firefox and Safari don't support it (official claim)
mwg:local-network-access.story: Home devices only speak http, while web pages are always https, so the two can't connect. Declare "I'm connecting to the LAN" up front and the browser lets it through after asking the user, also checking the hostname didn't resolve to the public internet.
mwg:local-network-access.unlock: Setup pages for smart appliances, 3D printers, or NAS boxes can be public https web pages that reach the device in the user's home, with no desktop app and no typing an IP into an http page. Chromium-only for now.
mwg:local-network-access.support: Local network access: Limited (Chrome 145, Edge 145; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:local-network-access:2.title: Send LAN requests only after a user click, not on load or from a Service Worker
mwg:local-network-access:2.action: Check state with `navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'local-network' })` first: connect if `granted`; if `prompt`, explain why and trigger from a button click; if `denied`, show how to re-enable it in site settings; always serve the page over https
mwg:local-network-access:2.blocker: Sending the first permission-gated request from a Service Worker or Shared Worker fails immediately because there's no attached Document; insecure http top-level pages are denied outright (quote: "never initiate the first permission-triggering request from a **Service Worker** or **Shared Worker** (which lack an attached `Document` and will immediately fail if permission is not already `'granted'`).")
mwg:local-network-access:2.outcome: Requests come from a user gesture, so the permission prompt can appear and make sense; unsupported browsers have no such permission (official claim)
mwg:local-network-access:2.story: Connecting to the LAN on load shows a permission prompt before users know why; doing it in a worker is worse, failing with no prompt at all. Check the state first, let the user press a button, then send the request.
mwg:local-network-access:2.support: Same as mwg:local-network-access; recorded as Limited

mwg:local-network-access:3.title: Don't query the legacy `'local-network-access'` permission name: older Chrome crashes the whole tab
mwg:local-network-access:3.action: Query only the granular `'local-network'`/`'loopback-network'` names, wrapped in `try/catch`, treating an unrecognized name as `'prompt'`
mwg:local-network-access:3.blocker: Querying the legacy combined name crashes the renderer process in older Chrome, and `try/catch` can't prevent it (quote: "In older Chrome versions this query crashes the renderer process, and `try / catch` cannot prevent it.")
mwg:local-network-access:3.outcome: Querying only the granular names, browsers that don't recognize them throw a `TypeError` that gets caught, and the request still runs on a user click (official claim)
mwg:local-network-access:3.story: Querying one extra old name "for compatibility" ends up crashing the tab in older Chrome. Use only the new names and the exception is caught normally.
mwg:local-network-access:3.support: Same as mwg:local-network-access; recorded as Limited

mwg:local-network-access:4.title: `WebSocket` doesn't take `{ targetAddressSpace }`; it's recognized from the URL itself
mwg:local-network-access:4.action: Pass only subprotocols as the second argument to `new WebSocket(url, protocols)`; use private/loopback IP literals, `localhost`, or `.local` hostnames so the browser recognizes them from the URL; use `wss://` for local endpoints with custom DNS names; don't pass `targetAddressSpace` to `WebTransport` either
mwg:local-network-access:4.blocker: Passing a `{ targetAddressSpace }` object as `WebSocket`'s second argument throws a `SyntaxError` (quote: "do **not** pass a `{ targetAddressSpace }` options object, which throws a `SyntaxError`.")
mwg:local-network-access:4.outcome: With a recognizable URL, `ws://` connections are exempted from mixed-content blocking after permission (official claim)
mwg:local-network-access:4.story: `fetch` needs the address space declared, but carrying that over to `WebSocket` throws immediately. WebSocket decides from what the URL looks like, not from options.
mwg:local-network-access:4.support: Same as mwg:local-network-access; recorded as Limited

mwg:local-network-access:5.title: Cross-origin iframes need `allow` and `Permissions-Policy` delegation to reach the LAN
mwg:local-network-access:5.action: Use `<iframe allow="local-network; loopback-network">` and send `Permissions-Policy: local-network=(self "https://partner…")` on the **embedding** document's response
mwg:local-network-access:5.blocker: Both permissions default to a `'self'` allowlist, so embedded cross-origin iframes can't make local or loopback requests (quote: "`local-network` and `loopback-network` have a default allowlist of `'self'`, blocking cross-origin `<iframe>` embeds from making local or loopback requests.")
mwg:local-network-access:5.outcome: With explicit delegation, hardware-setup widgets and SSO iframes that talk to a local agent can connect (official claim)
mwg:local-network-access:5.story: A partner's device-setup page is embedded in an iframe and can't reach the user's device. Only when the outer page explicitly delegates does the iframe get the permission.
mwg:local-network-access:5.support: Same as mwg:local-network-access; recorded as Limited

mwg:passkey-authentication.title: Use conditional mediation (`mediation: "conditional"`) to put passkeys in form autofill
mwg:passkey-authentication.action: The server returns discoverable-credential options with `allowCredentials: []`; mark fields `autocomplete="username webauthn"`; on load confirm `conditionalGet` via `PublicKeyCredential.getClientCapabilities()`, then call `navigator.credentials.get()` with `mediation: "conditional"` and an `AbortController`; also provide a "Sign in with passkey" button
mwg:passkey-authentication.blocker: The guide only says discoverable credentials spare users from entering a username first and let the provider list accounts, without saying when a username-first flow goes wrong (quote: "This requests discoverable credentials, meaning the user does not need to enter their username first; the passkey provider will present available accounts.")
mwg:passkey-authentication.outcome: Supporting browsers offer passkeys as soon as the user focuses the field; without `conditionalGet` the step is skipped, and `getClientCapabilities()` and JSON parsing can be filled in with `webauthn-polyfills` (official claim)
mwg:passkey-authentication.story: Open the sign-in page and the username field's autofill menu already has the passkey; one tap signs you in, no typing a username first. Unsupported environments keep using the password form.
mwg:passkey-authentication.unlock: A personal site or small tool can offer a single username field where users sign in with one tap using the passkey on their phone or computer, without designing a password-reset flow.
mwg:passkey-authentication.support: getClientCapabilities(): Newly (2025-02-06; Chrome 133, Edge 133, Firefox 135, Safari 17.4); parseRequestOptionsFromJSON(): Newly (2025-03-31)

mwg:passkey-authentication:2.title: Abort the background conditional request before a button sign-in, so two prompts don't collide
mwg:passkey-authentication:2.action: When "Sign in with passkey" is pressed, `abort()` the pending conditional `get()` and create a fresh `AbortController`; re-arm conditional autofill after a cancelled button flow; treat `NotAllowedError` and `AbortError` as expected
mwg:passkey-authentication:2.blocker: Firing an explicit passkey prompt while the background conditional request is still pending makes the two collide (quote: "Abort any pending Conditional Get call to prevent passkey prompt collisions")
mwg:passkey-authentication:2.outcome: Only one passkey request is in flight at a time (official claim)
mwg:passkey-authentication:2.story: The autofill request is waiting in the background, the user presses the button, and two WebAuthn requests fight. Cancel the background one first, and re-arm it afterwards.
mwg:passkey-authentication:2.support: Same as above; recorded as Newly

mwg:passkey-authentication:3.title: When the server doesn't know a credential, tell the password manager with `signalUnknownCredential()`
mwg:passkey-authentication:3.action: Return an explicit HTTP 404 when the credential ID isn't found; on the client, only on a 404 while unauthenticated, call `PublicKeyCredential.signalUnknownCredential({ rpId: publicKey.rpId, credentialId: encoded.id })` after feature detection
mwg:passkey-authentication:3.blocker: The guide only says the Signal API keeps password managers in sync with the server's credential state, without saying when being out of sync goes wrong (quote: "The WebAuthn Signal API (`webauthn-signals`) is a progressive optimization used to keep password managers in sync with the server credential state.")
mwg:passkey-authentication:3.outcome: Supporting browsers tell the provider about passkeys the server no longer recognizes; Firefox doesn't support it and the sync is safely skipped (official claim)
mwg:passkey-authentication:3.story: A passkey the server already deleted is still sitting in the user's password manager. Return 404 at sign-in and the browser can notify the provider to deal with it.
mwg:passkey-authentication:3.unlock: Sites can actively clean up stale passkeys in users' password managers, so after an account deletion or credential revocation users no longer see an option that's guaranteed to fail. Not supported in Firefox.
mwg:passkey-authentication:3.support: Web authentication signal methods: Limited (Chrome 132, Edge 132, Safari 26; not Firefox)

mwg:passkey-authentication:4.title: Keep the user-verification level in the server session, not sent back from the client
mwg:passkey-authentication:4.action: Store the `userVerification` level in the server session when generating options; the verification endpoint decides `requireUserVerification` from the session value
mwg:passkey-authentication:4.blocker: Passing the verification level back from the client (e.g. in a query string) effectively lets the client decide whether biometrics or a PIN are checked (quote: "The requested `userVerification` constraint level MUST be persisted inside the server session record at the options endpoint, rather than passed back from the client via query strings. This allows the verification endpoint to enforce strict matching constraints safely without risk of client manipulation.")
mwg:passkey-authentication:4.outcome: The server controls the verification requirement, free from client tampering (official claim)
mwg:passkey-authentication:4.story: If the "PIN required" setting comes back from the browser, changing a parameter skips it. Stored on the server, verification compares against its own record.
mwg:passkey-authentication:4.support: Same as above; recorded as Newly

mwg:passkey-conditional-create.title: After a successful password sign-in, quietly create a passkey with `mediation: 'conditional'`
mwg:passkey-conditional-create.action: Only after a full sign-in that involved a password and passed all factors: `abort()` the autofill conditional `get()`, confirm `capabilities.conditionalCreate`, then call `navigator.credentials.create()` with `mediation: 'conditional'` (with existing credentials in `excludeCredentials`); silently swallow `InvalidStateError`, `NotAllowedError`, and `AbortError`; relax the server's user-presence (UP) check only for these requests
mwg:passkey-conditional-create.blocker: The regular creation flow interrupts the user with an obtrusive modal dialog (quote: "This signals the browser to handle the passkey creation flow silently in the background or contextually without throwing obtrusive modal dialogs.")
mwg:passkey-conditional-create.outcome: Supporting platforms create the passkey in the background or in context without a modal; when `conditionalCreate` isn't available it's simply skipped (official claim)
mwg:passkey-conditional-create.story: A user who just signed in with a password, shown a big "Create a passkey?" dialog, mostly closes it. With conditional creation the browser saves one for them without interrupting, and next time they can sign in with a passkey.
mwg:passkey-conditional-create.unlock: Existing password-based sites don't need an "upgrade to passkeys" onboarding page: users sign in as usual and next time there's a passkey option waiting.
mwg:passkey-conditional-create.support: getClientCapabilities(): Newly (2025-02-06); parseCreationOptionsFromJSON(): Newly (2025-03-31). The guide gives no support data for conditional create itself; recorded as Newly

mwg:passkey-conditional-create:2.title: When server verification fails, clear the orphaned credential with `signalUnknownCredential()`
mwg:passkey-conditional-create:2.action: If `create()` succeeds but the server verification response isn't OK or the network fails, call `PublicKeyCredential.signalUnknownCredential({ rpId: publicKey.rp.id, credentialId: encodedResponse.id })`; server options must include `rp.id`
mwg:passkey-conditional-create:2.blocker: Credentials the server didn't accept linger in the passkey provider as orphans (quote: "invoke `PublicKeyCredential.signalUnknownCredential(…)` to prevent orphaned credentials from lingering in the passkey provider.")
mwg:passkey-conditional-create:2.outcome: Supporting browsers tell the provider to remove the orphan; Firefox doesn't support it and the sync is skipped (official claim)
mwg:passkey-conditional-create:2.story: The browser has already created the passkey but the server failed verification and didn't store it, so the user will later see an option that can never sign in. Notify the provider the moment verification fails.
mwg:passkey-conditional-create:2.unlock: Same as mwg:passkey-authentication:3: a failed registration doesn't leave a broken passkey in the user's password manager. Not supported in Firefox.
mwg:passkey-conditional-create:2.support: Web authentication signal methods: Limited (Chrome 132, Edge 132, Safari 26; not Firefox)

mwg:passkey-management.title: Use `signalAllAcceptedCredentials()` and `signalCurrentUserDetails()` to keep password managers in step with the server
mwg:passkey-management.action: Call `signalAllAcceptedCredentials({ rpId, userId, allAcceptedCredentialIds })` when the management page loads and after deleting a credential; call `signalCurrentUserDetails()` after the user changes their username or display name; renaming a passkey's nickname only updates the server; show each row's AAGUID-derived provider name and icon plus created and last-used dates
mwg:passkey-management.blocker: The guide only says the Signal API keeps synced vaults and the backend database consistent, without saying when being out of sync goes wrong (quote: "The Signal API lets the application communicate credential states to password managers, keeping the user's synced vaults and your backend database in lockstep.")
mwg:passkey-management.outcome: Supporting browsers sync server-side deletions and profile updates to the password manager; Firefox doesn't support it and it can't be polyfilled, while server-side management keeps working (official claim)
mwg:passkey-management.story: The user deletes a passkey and renames their account on the site's settings page, but their phone's password manager still shows the old ones. Signal on load, on delete, and on rename, and the two sides match.
mwg:passkey-management.unlock: An account settings page can make "delete it here and it disappears from the password manager on your phone; rename it here and the sign-in menu shows the new name" work without asking users to clean up their password manager. Not supported in Firefox.
mwg:passkey-management.support: Web authentication signal methods: Limited (Chrome 132, Edge 132, Safari 26; not Firefox)

mwg:passkey-management:2.title: Use the server-provided `rpId` for the Signal API, not `window.location.hostname`
mwg:passkey-management:2.action: Have the list and account-update endpoints return the server's configured `rpId`, and use it directly when calling the Signal API
mwg:passkey-management:2.blocker: When credentials are registered to a parent domain or shared via Related Origin Requests, `window.location.hostname` doesn't match, so sync silently targets the wrong RP ID or throws a `SecurityError` (quote: "`window.location.hostname` will not match the credential's RP ID, causing password manager synchronization to silently target the wrong RP ID or throw a `SecurityError`.")
mwg:passkey-management:2.outcome: With the server's RP ID, sync reaches the right set of credentials (official claim)
mwg:passkey-management:2.story: The settings page is at `accounts.example.com` but the passkeys are registered to `example.com`. Use the current hostname as the RP ID and the signal goes nowhere.
mwg:passkey-management:2.support: Same as mwg:passkey-management; recorded as Limited

mwg:passkey-management:3.title: IDs passed to the Signal API must be valid Base64URL, and failures should only `console.warn`
mwg:passkey-management:3.action: Store every `userId` and credential ID (including prototype seed data and mock backends) as unpadded Base64URL; validate before calling and skip invalid ones; wrap Signal API calls in `try/catch` and log failures with `console.warn`, not `console.error`
mwg:passkey-management:3.blocker: Passing human-readable mock IDs like `'passkey-1'` throws a `TypeError` on page load; logging passive sync failures with `console.error` fails Lighthouse's `errors-in-console` check (quote: "Passing arbitrary human-readable placeholder or mock IDs (…) throws `TypeError: Invalid base64url string for allAcceptedCredentialIds` on page load.")
mwg:passkey-management:3.outcome: Malformed IDs are skipped safely and sync failures don't break the page (official claim)
mwg:passkey-management:3.story: Readable mock data used during development goes unnoticed until launch, when the Signal API blows up the page on load. Validate first and downgrade failures to warnings, so background sync really stays in the background.
mwg:passkey-management:3.support: Same as mwg:passkey-management; recorded as Limited

mwg:passkey-reauthentication.title: Restrict `allowCredentials` to the current user's credentials on reauthentication, and have the server check the owner
mwg:passkey-reauthentication.action: Before sensitive actions (password change, transfers), the server fills `allowCredentials` with all of the signed-in user's credential IDs (with `transports`); the verification endpoint confirms the returned credential belongs to the current user (`storedCredential.passkeyUserId === req.user.id`) and rejects it otherwise
mwg:passkey-reauthentication.blocker: Leaving `allowCredentials` empty or omitting it falls back to discoverable credentials and breaks session safety; a different user's valid passkey may come back (quote: "Leaving this empty or omitting it regresses to discoverable credentials, violating session safety.")
mwg:passkey-reauthentication.outcome: The passkey prompt lists only the current user's credentials, and someone else's passkey is rejected by the server (official claim)
mwg:passkey-reauthentication.story: A signed-in user goes to make a transfer, and the passkey menu lists every account on the device; picking the wrong one might even pass. Restrict the list and check the owner on the server, so it really is the same person.
mwg:passkey-reauthentication.support: getClientCapabilities(): Newly (2025-02-06); parseRequestOptionsFromJSON(): Newly (2025-03-31). Recorded as Newly

mwg:passkey-registration.title: Use `excludeCredentials` to block duplicate passkeys on the same provider
mwg:passkey-registration.action: Put the user's existing credential IDs (with `transports`) in `excludeCredentials` when generating creation options; treat `InvalidStateError` on the client as "a passkey already exists" and tell the user
mwg:passkey-registration.blocker: Without an exclusion list, duplicate credentials get registered on the same passkey provider account (quote: "This prevents the authenticator from registering duplicate credentials on the same passkey provider account.")
mwg:passkey-registration.outcome: If a passkey already exists, creation ends with `InvalidStateError` instead of registering a duplicate (official claim)
mwg:passkey-registration.story: The user presses "Create passkey" once more on the settings page and the provider gains an identical entry. List existing ones for exclusion and the browser simply says one already exists.

mwg:passkey-registration:2.title: With `userVerification: "preferred"`, configure server verification with `requireUserVerification: false`
mwg:passkey-registration:2.action: When creation options use `"preferred"`, set `requireUserVerification: false` in the server-side verification library, while still requiring the user-present (UP) flag to be `true`
mwg:passkey-registration:2.blocker: If the options "prefer" verification but the server "requires" it, authenticators without a screen lock fail verification spuriously (quote: "Otherwise, authenticators that register without user verification (e.g., screen locks disabled) will trigger spurious server verification failures.")
mwg:passkey-registration:2.outcome: Front-end and back-end verification requirements match, and spurious verification failures stop (official claim)
mwg:passkey-registration:2.story: The browser finishes registration as "preferred" while the server verifies as "required"; the two aren't talking about the same thing, and users see baffling failures.
mwg:passkey-registration:2.support: Same as above; recorded as Newly

mwg:passkeys.title: The server decides the RP ID and passes it to the client; the client doesn't infer it from the URL
mwg:passkeys.action: The RP ID in server options must equal the current origin's domain, be a valid registrable parent of it, or be authorized via `/.well-known/webauthn`; the client (including Signal API calls) always reads `publicKey.rp.id`/`publicKey.rpId` or the backend response
mwg:passkeys.blocker: A mismatched RP ID throws `SecurityError` on the client; a value inferred from `window.location.hostname` won't match a parent-domain or related-origin configuration (quote: "Mismatches result in `SecurityError` exceptions on the client side.")
mwg:passkeys.outcome: The guide has no support data and doesn't say how far the errors go away when followed (official claim)
mwg:passkeys.story: Passkeys are bound to an RP ID. With the sign-in page on a subdomain and credentials bound to the parent domain, a client guessing from the URL will guess wrong.
mwg:passkeys.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:passkeys:2.title: Use the AAGUID only to show the provider name and icon, never for security decisions
mwg:passkeys:2.action: Use the AAGUID only for UX hints (showing which passkey provider in a management list), never for cryptographic security or access-control decisions
mwg:passkeys:2.blocker: Platform passkeys' AAGUIDs aren't cryptographically attested and can be altered or simulated by user agents (quote: "Platform passkeys do not currently provide cryptographic attestation for their AAGUIDs, meaning it can be altered or simulated by user agents.")
mwg:passkeys:2.outcome: Not treating a forgeable value as a security basis removes the risk of being impersonated through it (official claim)
mwg:passkeys:2.story: Seeing an AAGUID for a particular hardware key, you might want to allow only that vendor; but the value can be faked. It's only fit for telling users "this one is from iCloud Keychain".
mwg:passkeys:2.support: No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:quick-sign-ins.title: Use `uiMode: 'immediate'` to sign in in place instead of sending users to a sign-in page
mwg:quick-sign-ins.action: In click handlers for a "Sign in" link, "Proceed to checkout", favorite/like, or an article paywall, call `navigator.credentials.get({ password: true, publicKey, uiMode: 'immediate' })` (no `signal`, no `allowCredentials`); branch on `cred.type` to passkey or password verification; on `NotAllowedError`, fall back to the regular sign-in flow with a path back to the original action
mwg:quick-sign-ins.blocker: Sending users to a dedicated sign-in page when they click "Sign in", start checkout, favorite something, or hit a paywall loses their context and increases drop-off (quote: "Navigating an unauthenticated user to a dedicated sign-in page when they click a "Sign in" link, start checkout, save an item to favorites, or reach an article paywall causes context loss and increases user drop-off.")
mwg:quick-sign-ins.outcome: When the device has local passkeys or saved passwords, a unified account chooser lets users sign in in place with one tap; otherwise it fails fast and returns to the original flow. It must be detected with `capabilities.immediateGet`, password credentials are Chromium-only, and other browsers still go to the sign-in page (official claim)
mwg:quick-sign-ins.story: A reader taps favorite, gets taken to a sign-in page, and by the time they're back has forgotten what they meant to save. Immediate mode signs people with credentials in place and finishes the action, while those without bounce straight back to the usual flow instead of getting stuck on a QR-code dialog.
mwg:quick-sign-ins.unlock: Content sites' favorite, comment, and continue-reading buttons can complete sign-in plus the action in place, so returning readers never leave the article; people without credentials still see the usual sign-in form. Actual support is determined by runtime detection.
mwg:quick-sign-ins.support: Password credentials: Limited (Chrome 60, Edge 79; not Firefox or Safari). For immediate mode itself the guide gives only a runtime check (`capabilities.immediateGet`), no support data; getClientCapabilities(): Newly

mwg:quick-sign-ins:2.title: Don't use immediate mode on the dedicated sign-in page, or the button does nothing
mwg:quick-sign-ins:2.action: On the final sign-in page, use Conditional UI (`mediation: 'conditional'` with `autocomplete="username webauthn"`) plus a regular modal `get()` button; reserve immediate mode for the moment right before leaving the current page
mwg:quick-sign-ins:2.blocker: People who reach the dedicated sign-in page usually have no local credentials or want to scan a QR code or use a hardware key, but immediate mode suppresses those options and throws `NotAllowedError` immediately without local credentials (quote: "using it on a dedicated sign-in page traps the user in a dead end where clicking the button does nothing.")
mwg:quick-sign-ins:2.outcome: The sign-in page keeps cross-device and security-key options, so users don't get stuck (official claim)
mwg:quick-sign-ins:2.story: Put the smoothest button on the sign-in page and it meets exactly the people who most need a QR code, and nothing happens when they press it. Immediate mode is for intercepting, not for the destination.
mwg:quick-sign-ins:2.support: Same as mwg:quick-sign-ins; recorded as Limited

mwg:quick-sign-ins:3.title: Always check `capabilities.immediateGet` first; don't guess from the browser version
mwg:quick-sign-ins:3.action: Before calling immediate mode, confirm `immediateGet` via `PublicKeyCredential.getClientCapabilities()`; when unsupported, treat it as `NotAllowedError` and go to the existing sign-in flow
mwg:quick-sign-ins:3.blocker: Browsers that don't recognize `uiMode: 'immediate'` ignore the key and open a blocking passkey and QR-code dialog instead (quote: "browsers that do not recognize `uiMode: 'immediate'` ignore the unknown dictionary key and open a blocking modal passkey and QR code dialog.")
mwg:quick-sign-ins:3.outcome: With detection, unsupported browsers see the existing sign-in flow rather than a sudden blocking dialog (official claim)
mwg:quick-sign-ins:3.story: The plan was "sign in in place if possible, otherwise never mind"; in unsupported browsers it became "everyone gets interrupted by a QR-code dialog". Ask about the capability first, then decide whether to call.
mwg:quick-sign-ins:3.support: Same as mwg:quick-sign-ins; recorded as Limited

mwg:quick-sign-ins:4.title: Don't use immediate mode for reauthentication, or a different account may be chosen
mwg:quick-sign-ins:4.action: For reauthentication before changing a password, address, or payment method, or adding a passkey, follow `passkey-reauthentication` with a non-empty `allowCredentials`
mwg:quick-sign-ins:4.blocker: Immediate mode rejects a non-empty `allowCredentials`, and omitting it lets users unknowingly pick an account other than the one signed in (quote: "omitting `allowCredentials` would let the user inadvertently select a different account than the one currently signed in.")
mwg:quick-sign-ins:4.outcome: Reauthentication stays limited to the current user's credentials (official claim)
mwg:quick-sign-ins:4.story: For privacy, immediate mode forbids naming credentials, which is exactly the opposite of what reauthentication needs: it must be this person.
mwg:quick-sign-ins:4.support: Same as mwg:quick-sign-ins; recorded as Limited

mwg:quick-sign-ins:5.title: When the sign-in trigger hides after in-place sign-in, return focus to the original action button
mwg:quick-sign-ins:5.action: When in-place sign-in (or fallback form submission) hides the sign-in trigger, move focus back to the originating action control (or a surviving signed-in control in the header) and announce the signed-in state in `role="status"`; when revealing an inline fallback form, move focus to its first field
mwg:quick-sign-ins:5.blocker: When the sign-in trigger or inline form is hidden, keyboard focus drops to `document.body` (quote: "restore focus to the originating action control (…) so keyboard focus does not drop to `document.body`")
mwg:quick-sign-ins:5.outcome: Keyboard users stay on the original action and hear the signed-in state (official claim)
mwg:quick-sign-ins:5.story: Tap favorite, sign in in place, the "Sign in" button disappears and focus goes with it, so keyboard users have to Tab from the header again. Put focus back on the favorite button and the action stays continuous.
mwg:quick-sign-ins:5.support: Same as mwg:quick-sign-ins; recorded as Limited

mwg:restrict-outbound-connections.title: Use `Connection-Allowlist` to govern all outbound connections with one list, including channels CSP misses
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections.action: Send `Connection-Allowlist: (response-origin "https://api.example.com" …); report-to=…` on document and worker-script responses with `Reporting-Endpoints` and `Vary: Sec-Fetch-Dest`; give Dedicated/Shared Workers the same list and the Service Worker a superset of all controlled documents; optionally send `-Report-Only` alongside to trial a stricter list
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections.blocker: CSP needs separate per-resource directives and doesn't cover speculative or non-Fetch channels like `dns-prefetch`, `preconnect`, or WebRTC, and compromised page scripts can still exfiltrate via `worker.postMessage()` (quote: "does not govern speculative or non-Fetch network channels such as `<link rel="dns-prefetch">`, `<link rel="preconnect">`, or WebRTC")
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections.outcome: Supporting browsers apply a single list to every outbound connection at the network layer, blocking redirects and WebRTC by default; it can't be polyfilled, so Firefox and Safari fall back to CSP and the channels CSP misses stay open (official claim)
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections.story: With CSP in place, data can still slip out through DNS prefetch, preconnect, or WebRTC. Listing "only these destinations" at the network layer covers every channel at once; for now only Chromium enforces it.
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections.unlock: Tools whose data should never leave the page, like a password generator, local notes, or a wallet, can declare in a response header that they only talk to themselves (or cut everything with `()` after load), so users or auditors can confirm they don't phone home. Chromium-only for now.
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections.support: Connection allowlists: Limited (Chrome 152, Edge 152; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:2.title: Get the list syntax or defaults wrong and legitimate connections get blocked too
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:2.action: Write the header as an RFC 9651 Inner List `(...)` with space-separated items and unquoted `response-origin` and parameters; drop the trailing slash on origin-only patterns or use `/*`; rewrite `ws(s)://` as `http(s)://`; include external navigation targets (OAuth, payments); add `; redirects=allow` or `; webrtc=allow` when needed; wrap client `fetch` in `try/catch` to show a blocked state
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:2.blocker: If a non-empty header fails to parse, the browser fails closed with an empty list and blocks all outbound connections; the trailing slash `new URL()` adds limits a pattern to the root path; by default even same-origin 3xx redirects are blocked (quote: "the browser fails closed with an empty allowlist and blocks **all** outbound network connections.")
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:2.outcome: With correct syntax and patterns and the defaults opened deliberately, legitimate APIs, CDNs, navigations, and redirects work normally (official claim)
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:2.story: One missing pair of parentheses or one extra slash and every request on the page fails, or only the root path gets through. This header responds to mistakes by shutting everything, so generate it to spec and watch it in Report-Only first.
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:2.support: Same as mwg:restrict-outbound-connections; recorded as Limited

mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:3.title: When falling back to CSP, write `form-action` and `worker-src 'self'` explicitly
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:3.action: In browsers without `Connection-Allowlist`, pair with CSP: write `form-action` and `worker-src 'self'` (without `blob:`) explicitly, and list `wss://` origins in `connect-src`
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:3.blocker: `default-src` doesn't apply to `<form action>`; without restricting `worker-src`, a restricted page can spawn `blob:` SharedWorkers to bypass document-level restrictions (quote: "Include `worker-src 'self'` (excluding `blob:`) so restricted pages cannot spawn `blob:` SharedWorkers to bypass document-level restrictions.")
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:3.outcome: With these two added, form submissions and workers are no longer holes in CSP (official claim)
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:3.story: You assume `default-src 'self'` covers everything, yet forms can still post anywhere and workers can start their own operation. These two directives have to be written out.
mwg:restrict-outbound-connections:3.support: CSP: the guide only gives support data for Connection-Allowlist, not CSP; recorded as N/A

mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html.title: Use native `setHTML()` to parse, sanitize, and insert in one step
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html.action: Insert user-generated HTML with `element.setHTML(html)` (the default sanitizer removes scripts, event handlers, and anything outside its allowlist); pass `new Sanitizer({ elements, attributes, replaceWithChildrenElements })` to restrict further; use `Document.parseHTML()` to parse without inserting; dynamically load DOMPurify only where unsupported
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html.blocker: `<script>` tags and `on*` attributes in user-generated HTML execute once they reach the DOM (quote: "The native **Sanitizer API** provides a built-in, browser-optimized way to strip dangerous content (like `<script>` tags or `on*` attributes) before it reaches the DOM.")
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html.outcome: Supporting browsers sanitize built-in and for the insertion context; Safari doesn't support it and needs DOMPurify configured to match native behavior (official claim)
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html.story: Showing comments or a Markdown preview used to require shipping a sanitizer library. Now the browser sanitizes on its own and can't be configured to let XSS through; Safari still needs the library on standby.
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html.unlock: Comment sections, Markdown note previews, and email viewers can `setHTML()` user HTML directly without downloading a sanitizer in supporting browsers, or use `parseHTML()` to build a clean preview before deciding to insert. Safari still needs DOMPurify.
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html.support: Sanitizer API: Limited (Chrome 146, Edge 146, Firefox 148; not Safari)

mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:2.title: Move sanitized nodes directly; don't serialize to a string and feed it back into `innerHTML`
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:2.action: Move the result of `Document.parseHTML()` into the page with `replaceChildren(...doc.body.childNodes)`
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:2.blocker: Serializing sanitized nodes to a string and re-parsing with `innerHTML` can reintroduce mutation XSS (quote: "Move the resulting nodes into the page rather than serializing them to a string and re-parsing it with `innerHTML`, which can reintroduce mutation XSS (mXSS).")
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:2.outcome: Nodes are moved directly, so the sanitized result is never re-parsed and has no chance to mutate (official claim)
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:2.story: Turn clean content back into a string and parse it again, and the browser may parse it into a different structure; that's the gap attacks slip through.
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:2.support: Same as mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html; recorded as Limited

mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:3.title: Custom sanitizers delete content along with the element, and the DOMPurify fallback defaults differ
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:3.action: List wrapper elements whose text you want to keep in `replaceWithChildrenElements`; configure the DOMPurify fallback with `ALLOW_ARIA_ATTR: false`, `ALLOW_DATA_ATTR: false`, `KEEP_CONTENT: false` and allow `#text`; avoid `replaceWithChildrenElements` in configurations that need a matching fallback
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:3.blocker: Elements not in `elements` are removed together with their content; DOMPurify by default keeps `aria-*`, `data-*`, and the text of removed elements, so the two paths produce different output (quote: "Elements that are not in `elements` are removed **together with their content**.")
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:3.outcome: Once configured, native and fallback produce the same result, and text you meant to keep doesn't vanish (official claim)
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:3.story: Allow only a few inline tags and a whole paragraph wrapped in `<div>` disappears; switch to the DOMPurify fallback in Safari and a pile of attributes shows up. The two have to be aligned on purpose.
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:3.support: Same as mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html; recorded as Limited

mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:4.title: With Trusted Types enforced, the DOMPurify fallback must return TrustedHTML
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:4.action: Pass `RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE: true` to `DOMPurify.sanitize()` in the fallback and allow the `dompurify` policy name in the `trusted-types` CSP directive
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:4.blocker: With Trusted Types enforced, assigning a string to `innerHTML` throws (quote: "If the page enforces Trusted Types (`require-trusted-types-for 'script'`), assigning a string to `innerHTML` throws.")
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:4.outcome: `setHTML()` needs no Trusted Types policy, and the fallback inserts fine once it returns TrustedHTML (official claim)
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:4.story: The native path sails through Trusted Types, while the fallback gets blocked by the page's own security policy for assigning a string.
mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html:4.support: Same as mwg:sanitize-untrusted-html; recorded as Limited

mwg:secure-external-subresources.title: Add `integrity` to external scripts and stylesheets and pin them to immutable versioned URLs
mwg:secure-external-subresources.action: At build or release time compute `sha384-` digests from known-good local files and put them in `integrity` on `<script>`, `<link rel="stylesheet|preload|modulepreload">`, and `fetch()`; use versioned or content-addressed URLs; list multiple digests when one URL may serve several valid payloads; for third-party scripts that update in place, skip `integrity` and use CSP or iframe sandboxing instead
mwg:secure-external-subresources.blocker: Referencing mutable URLs like `latest/` exposes the site to silent supply-chain changes; computing the hash at runtime from the remote file trusts whatever the remote returns (quote: "rather than mutable floating URLs (`latest/app.min.js`), which expose your site to silent supply-chain changes and break SRI as soon as the remote file updates.")
mwg:secure-external-subresources.outcome: If the bytes don't match the declared digest, the browser won't execute or apply them (official claim)
mwg:secure-external-subresources.story: The file on the CDN gets swapped, and the site loads and runs it anyway. Pin the version and write the hash, and any change in content is blocked.
mwg:secure-external-subresources.support: The guide says subresource-integrity and referrer-policy on `<link rel="stylesheet">` are "widely available across all browsers"; recorded as Widely

mwg:secure-external-subresources:2.title: If there's `integrity`, there must be `crossorigin`, or the resource is simply blocked
mwg:secure-external-subresources:2.action: When setting `integrity` on a cross-origin resource, also set `crossorigin="anonymous"` (or `use-credentials`) and make sure the server sends CORS headers
mwg:secure-external-subresources:2.blocker: Without `crossorigin`, the browser fetches in `no-cors` mode, gets an opaque response whose hash can't be verified, and blocks the resource (quote: "Omitting `crossorigin` causes the browser to fetch the resource in `no-cors` mode (producing an opaque response that cannot be hash-verified) and block the resource.")
mwg:secure-external-subresources:2.outcome: A CORS response can be hash-verified and loads normally (official claim)
mwg:secure-external-subresources:2.story: You add an integrity check and the file doesn't load at all, because the browser can't see the content to compare.
mwg:secure-external-subresources:2.support: Same as mwg:secure-external-subresources; recorded as Widely

mwg:secure-external-subresources:3.title: Use CSS `url()` `integrity()` / `cross-origin()` / `referrer-policy()` to verify resources loaded from stylesheets
mwg:secure-external-subresources:3.action: Inside `url("…")` for `@import`, `@font-face src`, `background-image`, `mask-image`, etc., add `cross-origin(anonymous) referrer-policy(no-referrer) integrity("sha384-…")`; quote the URL and use each modifier only once
mwg:secure-external-subresources:3.blocker: `background-image`, `content`, `border-image-source`, and `@import` fetch in `no-cors` mode by default, and the opaque response can't be hash-verified (quote: "`background-image`, `content`, `border-image-source`, and `@import` default to `no-cors` mode (producing an opaque response that cannot be hash-verified)")
mwg:secure-external-subresources:3.outcome: Supporting browsers can verify fonts, images, and imported stylesheets from CSS; `integrity()` is Chromium-only and Firefox supports none of the three modifiers, so elsewhere you can only swap `@import` for `<link>`, and fonts and images in CSS remain unverified (official claim)
mwg:secure-external-subresources:3.story: Every script in the HTML has SRI, but fonts and `@import`s pulled from a CDN inside stylesheets couldn't be verified. Now you can put the hash inside `url()`, though for now only Chromium checks it.
mwg:secure-external-subresources:3.unlock: A design system published from a CDN can pin hashes on its fonts, icon sprites, and theme-token files right in the CSS, without splitting `@import`s into many `<link>`s for SRI. Only Chromium verifies for now.
mwg:secure-external-subresources:3.support: cross-origin() for url(): Limited (Chrome 150, Edge 150, Safari 26.2; not Firefox); referrer-policy() for url(): same; integrity() for url(): Limited (Chrome 150, Edge 150; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:secure-external-subresources:4.title: Don't put an unverified fallback in the same `@font-face` `src` list
mwg:secure-external-subresources:4.action: Do progressive enhancement with **separate** `src:` declarations: first a plain `url()`, then a version with only `cross-origin()`/`referrer-policy()`, and finally the version with `integrity()`
mwg:secure-external-subresources:4.blocker: With verified and unverified URLs in one comma-separated `src`, a tampered font from the CDN fails the check, is treated as a load failure, and the browser falls back to the second, unverified URL (quote: "in a single `src` descriptor bypasses Subresource Integrity at runtime")
mwg:secure-external-subresources:4.outcome: Supporting browsers overwrite the unverified declarations at parse time and block tampered fonts at runtime (official claim)
mwg:secure-external-subresources:4.story: An extra fallback for compatibility turns into a back door: once verification fails, the browser obligingly loads the same file unverified.
mwg:secure-external-subresources:4.support: Same as mwg:secure-external-subresources:3; recorded as Limited

mwg:secure-external-subresources:5.title: Set `referrerpolicy="no-referrer"` on external resources, with a document-level baseline policy
mwg:secure-external-subresources:5.action: Send `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (or `<meta name="referrer">`) as the document baseline; add `referrerpolicy="no-referrer"` to third-party CDN `<script>`/`<link>` elements and pass `referrerPolicy` to `fetch()`
mwg:secure-external-subresources:5.blocker: Requests to third-party hosts leak origin or path information in the `Referer` header (quote: "Overrides the document referrer policy to prevent leaking any origin or path information in the `Referer` request header to the third-party host.")
mwg:secure-external-subresources:5.outcome: Third-party hosts receive no origin or path; resources that omit it still have path and query stripped by the document-level policy (official claim)
mwg:secure-external-subresources:5.story: Every file loaded from a CDN also tells the CDN which page the user is reading. Turn it off per resource, and let the document-level policy catch the rest.
mwg:secure-external-subresources:5.support: Same as mwg:secure-external-subresources; recorded as Widely

mwg:security.title: Replace script domain allowlists with a nonce plus `'strict-dynamic'`
mwg:security.action: Use a fresh per-request nonce (script hashes for static HTML) with `'strict-dynamic'` and `'report-sample'` in CSP `script-src`, alongside `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'none'`, and `frame-ancestors`; let third-party analytics load their dependencies through `'strict-dynamic'` instead of allowlisting their domain
mwg:security.blocker: Domain allowlists such as `https:` or `script-src https://cdn.example.com` as the primary defense can be bypassed through open redirects, JSONP endpoints, or dependency injection on the allowed origin (quote: "they are easily bypassed by open redirects, JSONP endpoints, and dependency injection on the allowed origin.")
mwg:security.outcome: Only scripts carrying this response's nonce (and what they load) can run, so a hole on an allowlisted domain is no longer a free pass; the guide calls this the primary mechanism to prevent XSS (official claim)
mwg:security.story: An allowlist looks strict but really trusts every endpoint on that domain. With a nonce, what you trust is the handful of `<script>` tags you wrote into this very response.
mwg:security.support: CSP: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:2.title: Hand nonces to your own scripts in the template, don't stamp them on with a regex
mwg:security:2.action: Generate a nonce per request in the server or SSR middleware with `crypto.getRandomValues()`, put it in the `Content-Security-Policy` header and pass it into the template rendering context so only developer-authored `<script>` tags receive it
mwg:security:2.blocker: Adding nonces to every `<script>` in already-rendered HTML with a regular expression cannot tell developer scripts from ones injected via reflected or stored HTML, so it authorizes the attacker's scripts (quote: "authorizing attacker-injected scripts under `script-src 'nonce-...'`.")
mwg:security:2.outcome: Nonces go only to trusted tags at render time; injected `<script>` tags never get one (official claim)
mwg:security:2.story: To ship CSP quickly, some sites scan the output and stamp every `<script>`. That hands CSP's core decision to a regex, and a regex can't tell friend from foe.
mwg:security:2.support: CSP nonce: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:3.title: Keep untrusted strings out of dangerous sinks and enforce it at runtime with Trusted Types
mwg:security:3.action: Set text with `textContent`/`innerText`; insert untrusted HTML with `setHTML()`; build elements with `document.createElement` or DOMParser instead of concatenating HTML strings; add `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` to CSP and route necessary sink writes through a named `trustedTypes.createPolicy()`, never a pass-through policy
mwg:security:3.blocker: Untrusted or unsanitized input written to the DOM through `innerHTML` or `setHTMLUnsafe` becomes DOM XSS; a pass-through policy that returns input unchanged neutralizes Trusted Types (quote: "**DO NOT**: Use `innerHTML` or `setHTMLUnsafe` with untrusted or unsanitized input.")
mwg:security:3.outcome: Trusted Types blocks raw string assignments to `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `document.write`, and `script.src` at runtime unless they pass through a named policy (official claim)
mwg:security:3.story: `innerHTML`, `eval`, and string `setTimeout` are the list you grep for. A source-level rule depends on people following it; Trusted Types turns the same rule into a runtime error.
mwg:security:3.support: This guide gives no Trusted Types support data; recorded as N/A (the `trusted-types` guide records Newly, see mwg:trusted-types)

mwg:security:4.title: Start HSTS with a short max-age and raise it gradually
mwg:security:4.action: Send `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload` to force HTTPS; in production start with a `max-age` of about 300 seconds and raise it step by step to a year
mwg:security:4.blocker: Sending a long `max-age` from day one means a misconfiguration makes the site unreachable in every browser that saw the header until the cache expires (quote: "A misconfigured HSTS with a long max-age can render the site permanently inaccessible until the cache expires in every browser that saw it.")
mwg:security:4.outcome: Starting short limits a lockout to the short cache lifetime; once raised, the same risk returns (official claim)
mwg:security:4.story: HSTS can't be taken back once sent; browsers remember it for a full year. So send five minutes first, make sure every subdomain keeps up with HTTPS, then lengthen it.
mwg:security:4.support: HSTS: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:5.title: Use the `__Host-` prefix and `HttpOnly` on session cookies
mwg:security:5.action: Name single-domain first-party session cookies `__Host-session` (requires `Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`), fall back to `__Secure-` otherwise; set `HttpOnly` on session and auth cookies and explicitly set `SameSite=Lax`
mwg:security:5.blocker: A session cookie without `HttpOnly` can be read by injected client-side scripts (quote: "Set `HttpOnly` (`httpOnly: true`) on session and authentication cookies so they cannot be read by injected client-side scripts")
mwg:security:5.outcome: `HttpOnly` keeps injected scripts away from the session cookie; the `__Host-` prefix protects against same-site and network attackers (official claim)
mwg:security:5.story: Once a page has XSS, any script that can read cookies can walk off with the session. Make the cookie unreachable to scripts and a big chunk of the damage disappears.
mwg:security:5.support: Cookie attributes and prefixes: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:6.title: Switch apps embedded in third-party pages to partitioned cookies
mwg:security:6.action: When the app is embedded as an iframe in third-party contexts, set cookies with `SameSite=None; Secure; Partitioned`
mwg:security:6.blocker: Relying on unpartitioned `SameSite=None` cookies, which are being systematically blocked for tracking prevention (quote: "Rely on unpartitioned `SameSite=None` — these are being systematically blocked for tracking prevention.")
mwg:security:6.outcome: The guide only says to use `Partitioned`; it doesn't say what happens to cookies in embedded contexts afterwards
mwg:security:6.story: Embedded widgets have long relied on third-party cookies to remember users, and browsers are closing that road. The way out the guide points to is partitioned cookies: one jar per embedding site.
mwg:security:6.unlock: When third-party cookies got blocked, comment boxes, support chats, and payment widgets embedded in other sites forgot their users → now partitioned cookies keep sign-in and preferences within each site without turning the widget into a cross-site tracker. Same CHIPS as mwg:privacy:7
mwg:security:6.support: CHIPS (Partitioned): the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:7.title: Pick a `frame-ancestors` tier per embedding need, and drop X-Frame-Options for cross-origin partners
mwg:security:7.action: No framing: `frame-ancestors 'none'` plus `X-Frame-Options: DENY`; same-origin only: `'self'` plus `SAMEORIGIN`; specific cross-origin partners: only `frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted-partner.com`, omitting `X-Frame-Options`
mwg:security:7.blocker: Still sending `X-Frame-Options: DENY` or `SAMEORIGIN` when cross-origin embedding is needed makes clients that evaluate XFO without `frame-ancestors` block the embed (quote: "`DENY` or `SAMEORIGIN` would block the embed in any client that evaluates `X-Frame-Options` without `frame-ancestors`")
mwg:security:7.outcome: Each tier has a matching recipe that blocks clickjacking without blocking legitimate partner embeds (official claim)
mwg:security:7.story: X-Frame-Options can only say block everything or same-origin only; `ALLOW-FROM` has long been unsupported. When you need to allow a specific partner, keeping XFO locks that partner out in some clients.
mwg:security:7.support: frame-ancestors, X-Frame-Options: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:8.title: Get cross-origin isolation with `Document-Isolation-Policy` instead of adding CORP to every subresource
mwg:security:8.action: Only isolate when `SharedArrayBuffer` is needed (e.g. WebAssembly threads); in Chromium prefer `Document-Isolation-Policy: isolate-and-credentialless`, which strips credentials from non-CORS cross-origin fetches instead of blocking them; use `isolate-and-require-corp` when blocking is wanted
mwg:security:8.blocker: The cross-browser path (`COOP: same-origin` plus `COEP: require-corp`) requires every embedded subresource to send a CORP header or the browser won't load it (quote: "Every embedded subresource (images, styles, external media) MUST serve an explicit `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` header or the browser will prevent it from loading.")
mwg:security:8.outcome: `Document-Isolation-Policy` lets cross-origin resources without CORP load (without credentials); but it is supported mainly in Chrome 142+ and other vendors haven't shown interest, so cross-browser isolation still goes through COEP (official claim)
mwg:security:8.story: Turning on isolation for SharedArrayBuffer used to mean every third-party image needed its host to add a header, or it broke. The new policy loads them without cookies instead, but only in Chrome for now.
mwg:security:8.unlock: Using SharedArrayBuffer used to require every third-party image, font, and video host to add CORP → now in-browser Wasm thread tools (video transcoding, local image processing) can enable isolation while still embedding outside assets. Mainly Chrome for now
mwg:security:8.support: Document-Isolation-Policy: the guide says "supported primarily in Chrome (142+) and other vendors have not yet shown interest"; recorded as Limited

mwg:security:9.title: Use Fetch Metadata to reject cross-site requests before authentication
mwg:security:9.action: On the server check `Sec-Fetch-Site`/`Sec-Fetch-Mode`/`Sec-Fetch-Dest`, reject `cross-site` requests to non-navigational endpoints before any authentication or authorization check; add `Vary: Sec-Fetch-Dest, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Site`; drop `same-site` from the allowlist if any subdomain hosts user content
mwg:security:9.blocker: Rejecting only after authentication leaks timing information about whether a resource or session exists; without `Vary`, an intermediate CDN may serve cached responses to attackers (quote: "Reject disallowed requests *before* authentication or authorization checks, so the response does not leak timing information about whether a resource or session exists.")
mwg:security:9.outcome: Rejecting early leaves no timing gap, and `Vary` makes caches separate responses by Fetch Metadata (official claim)
mwg:security:9.story: The cross-site request gets blocked, but if the block comes after looking up the account, an attacker can infer existence from response time alone. Reject first, then look up, and keep caches separated.
mwg:security:9.support: Fetch Metadata: the guide gives no browser support data (its example lets legacy browsers without `Sec-Fetch-Site` through); recorded as N/A

mwg:security:10.title: Credentialed CORS must echo a specific origin, not `*`
mwg:security:10.action: Validate the `Origin` request header on the server and set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` dynamically to that origin; handle `OPTIONS` preflight first
mwg:security:10.blocker: Setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to `*` when `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is required makes the browser reject the response (quote: "Use wildcard `*` for `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` if `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is required — the browser will reject the response.")
mwg:security:10.outcome: Echoing a validated origin makes credentialed cross-origin reads work without opening up to every origin (official claim)
mwg:security:10.story: CORS is a grant, not a defense, and the usual mistake is granting too much. The wildcard-plus-cookies combo is one the browser simply refuses to read.
mwg:security:10.support: CORS: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:11.title: Send a complete `Clear-Site-Data` on logout
mwg:security:11.action: Have the logout endpoint respond with `Clear-Site-Data: "cookies", "storage", "cache"`, all three directives
mwg:security:11.blocker: Omitting any one leaves active session cookies, Web Storage state, or cached authenticated pages in the browser (quote: "omitting any of these directives leaves active session cookies, Web Storage state, or cached authenticated pages behind.")
mwg:security:11.outcome: All three kinds of data are cleared together and the session fully ends (official claim)
mwg:security:11.story: The logout button was pressed and the server session deleted, yet the browser cache still holds the previous account page. The next person at a shared computer just presses Back.
mwg:security:11.support: Clear-Site-Data: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:12.title: Use SRI only on immutable, versioned assets
mwg:security:12.action: Add `integrity` (preferring `sha384`, `sha512`, or `sha256`) with `crossorigin="anonymous"` to third-party scripts and stylesheets, with the CDN sending `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`; only for pinned-version URLs
mwg:security:12.blocker: Putting SRI on dynamic or unversioned assets means the hash stops matching on the next silent update and the script fails to run (quote: "Use SRI for dynamic or unversioned assets — silent updates will cause script execution to fail.")
mwg:security:12.outcome: SRI pinned to fixed versions never breaks because upstream changed (official claim)
mwg:security:12.story: SRI exists precisely to refuse changed content, so binding it to an auto-updating file means the site breaks itself on the upstream's next release day.
mwg:security:12.support: SRI: this guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A (the `secure-external-subresources` guide records Widely)

mwg:trusted-types.title: Use Trusted Types so dangerous sinks only accept policy-made objects
mwg:trusted-types.action: Define sanitizing policies with `trustedTypes.createPolicy()` (delegating to DOMPurify or the app's escaping rules), convert to `TrustedHTML`/`TrustedScriptURL` before writing to sinks such as `innerHTML`, `document.write()`, `<script src>`, and `Worker()`; enforce with CSP `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` and restrict policy names with the `trusted-types` directive
mwg:trusted-types.blocker: These DOM APIs accept raw strings by default, so a string carrying malicious script from an untrusted source gets executed (quote: "If a string contains malicious script from an untrusted source, it can be executed.")
mwg:trusted-types.outcome: Under enforcement, string writes to sinks that skip a policy throw, and unlisted policies can't be created; `setHTML()` and `Document.parseHTML()` sanitize natively and need no policy. Trusted Types only became Baseline in 2026-02; older browsers run the sanitizing logic through a tinyfill but get no sink-level enforcement (official claim)
mwg:trusted-types.story: Asking everyone not to use `innerHTML` is one thing; guaranteeing no code path ever pushes a raw string into it is another. Trusted Types hands the latter to the browser: any stray write throws.
mwg:trusted-types.unlock: Confirming no `innerHTML` slipped through used to rely on code review and grep → now comment sections, Markdown previews, and CMS editors can have the browser guarantee across all four engines that any unsanitized write throws and gets reported
mwg:trusted-types.support: Trusted Types: Newly available (2026-02-24). Supported by: Chrome 83, Edge 83, Firefox 148, Safari 26

mwg:trusted-types:2.title: Collect violations in Report-Only first; enforce Trusted Types only once they reach zero
mwg:trusted-types:2.action: First confirm the framework and third-party libraries produce `TrustedHTML`/`TrustedScript`; send `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: require-trusted-types-for 'script'`, optionally registering a temporary `default` policy that logs where strings still arrive; switch to the enforcing `Content-Security-Policy` once reports drop to zero
mwg:trusted-types:2.blocker: Enforcing while some sink writes aren't migrated, or while the framework or libraries don't produce Trusted Types, breaks the application (quote: "it carries a risk of site breakage if every sink write hasn't been migrated.")
mwg:trusted-types:2.outcome: Report-Only logs without blocking, so sinks can be fixed one by one without breaking the site; enforcement is still impossible if the framework won't cooperate (official claim)
mwg:trusted-types:2.story: Trusted Types protects by always throwing, and the same trait can take the site down the moment it's switched on. Observe, fix, and only then enforce.
mwg:trusted-types:2.support: Same as mwg:trusted-types; recorded as Newly

mwg:trusted-types:3.title: Character escaping is not an HTML sanitizer
mwg:trusted-types:3.action: Use `element.textContent` (not a Trusted Types sink) when only plain text is needed; use a full sanitizer (DOMPurify or `element.setHTML()`) when accepting markup or attributes; never interpolate `escapePolicy.createHTML()` output into another HTML template
mwg:trusted-types:3.blocker: Interpolating character-escaped strings into unquoted attributes or URL attributes like `href` leaves `javascript:` URLs un-neutralized by entity escaping (quote: "a URL attribute (`<a href="${escaped}">`, where `javascript:` URLs are not neutralized by entity escaping)")
mwg:trusted-types:3.outcome: Plain text goes through `textContent`, markup through a full sanitizer, and escaped output is never used to build new HTML (official claim)
mwg:trusted-types:3.story: An escaping policy makes Trusted Types stop complaining, so it looks like the check passed. But `<` can't save you from `javascript:alert(1)`: it has no angle brackets to begin with.
mwg:trusted-types:3.support: Same as mwg:trusted-types; recorded as Newly

mwg:validate-origins.title: Replace string prefix checks with `Origin.from()` plus `isSameOrigin()`
mwg:validate-origins.action: For privileged actions such as cross-window `postMessage` commands or deciding whether to attach credentials, convert both sides to `Origin` objects with `Origin.from()` (MessageEvent, `<a>`, and URL can be passed directly) and compare scheme, host, and port with `isSameOrigin()`; wrap calls in try/catch so invalid URLs and "null" return false
mwg:validate-origins.blocker: A `startsWith()` prefix check is bypassed by `https://app.example.com.attacker.example`; full URLs with paths or explicit default ports don't match under string equality (quote: "Checking `url.startsWith('https://app.example.com')` is bypassed by `'https://app.example.com.attacker.example'`.")
mwg:validate-origins.outcome: Comparison happens after the browser's URL parser normalizes both sides, so prefix spoofing and port spelling no longer cause misjudgments; Firefox lacks support and must fall back to comparing `.origin` from `new URL()` after rejecting "null" (official claim)
mwg:validate-origins.story: Prefix checks always pass in tests, because nobody tests with `app.example.com.attacker.example`. With structured origin objects you compare the parsed triple, not whether strings look alike.
mwg:validate-origins.unlock: Every postMessage receiver used to parse URLs and handle default ports itself → now embedded checkouts, sign-in popups, and cross-window widgets can hand the event straight to `Origin.from()` and compare in one line. Not yet in Firefox
mwg:validate-origins.support: Origin: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 145, Edge 145, Safari 26.5. Unsupported in: Firefox

mwg:validate-origins:2.title: Use `isSameSite()` for cross-subdomain redirects and links
mwg:validate-origins:2.action: When validating post-login `?returnTo=` targets or classifying links as internal vs. external, convert with `Origin.from()` and call `isSameSite()` for a schemeful same-site comparison
mwg:validate-origins:2.blocker: Splitting hostnames on `.` to decide same-site gets multi-label public suffixes like `.co.uk` and `.github.io` wrong and ignores http vs. https (quote: "Splitting hostnames on `.` to check same-site relationships fails on multi-label public suffixes (such as `.co.uk` or shared hosting domains like `.github.io`) and ignores scheme mismatches (`http:` vs. `https:`).")
mwg:validate-origins:2.outcome: `isSameSite()` uses the browser's built-in Public Suffix List, so `tenant-a.github.io` and `tenant-b.github.io` count as different sites and http downgrades are rejected; in unsupported browsers `URL` has no PSL access, so you can only match domains you control or ship a PSL library (official claim)
mwg:validate-origins:2.story: Take the last two labels of `a.co.uk` and `b.co.uk` and both are `co.uk`, so they look like one site. The right answer was always inside the browser; it just wasn't exposed.
mwg:validate-origins:2.unlock: Correct same-site checks used to mean shipping a Public Suffix List to the front end → now services spread across subdomains (billing, help center, main site) can safely allow redirects between each other without being spoofed by neighbors on the same public suffix. Not in Firefox
mwg:validate-origins:2.support: Same as mwg:validate-origins; recorded as Limited

mwg:validate-origins:3.title: Tell sandboxed iframes apart with `Origin.from(event)`
mwg:validate-origins:3.action: When receiving messages from a sandboxed iframe (`sandbox="allow-scripts"`), extract the underlying opaque origin with `Origin.from(event)`, pin it once at initialization from the expected iframe, then compare with `isSameOrigin()`; use `new Origin()` as a match-nothing sentinel before pinning; reject redirect targets whose `origin.opaque` is true
mwg:validate-origins:3.blocker: Sandboxed iframes and `data:` URLs all serialize `event.origin` to the string "null", so comparing with `===` treats two unrelated opaque origins as the same (quote: "Comparing two serialized runtime origins with `originA === originB` falsely equates two unrelated opaque contexts (`"null" === "null"`).")
mwg:validate-origins:3.outcome: Messages from the same sandboxed iframe match each other and different iframes don't; in unsupported browsers `event.origin` is always "null", so check `event.source` or use a dedicated `MessageChannel` handed over at initialization (official claim)
mwg:validate-origins:3.story: Locking untrusted code inside a sandboxed iframe is a good idea, but every sandbox signs its mail "null". The new API lets the browser say whether this message came from the same sandbox as the last one.
mwg:validate-origins:3.unlock: Telling several sandboxed iframes on one page apart used to require `event.source` or a separate MessageChannel → now plugin systems, user code previews, and multiple third-party widgets can each live in a sandbox while their messages still map reliably to the sender. Not in Firefox
mwg:validate-origins:3.support: Same as mwg:validate-origins; recorded as Limited

mwg:validate-origins:4.title: Both sides of the `Origin` API must be `Origin` objects, and calls need try/catch
mwg:validate-origins:4.action: Run both sides through `Origin.from()` before comparing; get the current context's origin with `Origin.from(self)`; fall back to parsing `event.origin` for synthetic test `MessageEvent`s; wrap every call on runtime input in try/catch returning false
mwg:validate-origins:4.blocker: Passing a raw string to `isSameOrigin()`, passing `Location`/`Document` to `Origin.from()`, or synthesizing events with `new MessageEvent()` in unit tests all throw a `TypeError` (quote: "passing a raw string throws a `TypeError`.")
mwg:validate-origins:4.outcome: Written this way, invalid URLs, "null" strings, and unsupported objects safely return false instead of throwing uncaught errors (official claim)
mwg:validate-origins:4.story: The new API is stricter than strings, strict enough to throw on the wrong type. When an origin check throws, the whole message handler stops, so every call needs a fallback.
mwg:validate-origins:4.support: Same as mwg:validate-origins; recorded as Limited

mwg:verify-email-ownership.title: Confirm email ownership without sending mail, using `autocomplete="email-verification-token"`
mwg:verify-email-ownership.action: Put an `autocomplete="email"` field and a hidden `autocomplete="email-verification-token"` input carrying a server-side nonce in the same `<form>`; the browser checks the domain's DNS record, obtains an Email Verification Token from the email provider, binds it to the origin and nonce, and submits it; if the backend verifies it, skip the one-time code or magic link
mwg:verify-email-ownership.blocker: The traditional one-time code or magic link makes users leave the page, wait for mail, and copy codes, causing drop-off and phishing risk, and tells the email provider which site the user is visiting (quote: "This forces users to leave your page, wait for email delivery, and copy codes—introducing friction, drop-off, and phishing risk, while also revealing to the email provider which relying party (RP) the user is visiting.")
mwg:verify-email-ownership.outcome: With a supporting browser, a signed-in provider session, and a domain that publishes the DNS record, ownership is verified on the spot without the provider learning which site asked; but it currently requires an origin trial, and otherwise the field submits empty and you fall back to sending a verification email (official claim)
mwg:verify-email-ownership.story: Go check your inbox and type the six digits back is where sign-ups leak most. The browser is already signed into the mailbox, so the new protocol lets it present proof directly; when unsupported, the old flow takes over untouched.
mwg:verify-email-ownership.unlock: Verifying an email used to mean switching to the inbox and copying a code → now sign-up, checkout, and newsletter subscription can finish verification on the same page, almost frictionless for users of participating providers like Gmail. Chrome origin trial only for now
mwg:verify-email-ownership.support: Email Verification API: the guide gives no Baseline data, only says to enable an origin trial and mentions Chrome Origin Trial builds; recorded as Limited (Chrome origin trial only)

mwg:verify-email-ownership:2.title: Keep the verification nonce on the server and use it once
mwg:verify-email-ownership:2.action: Generate a nonce of at least 128 bits on the server for every form render, store it in server-side session state keyed by an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` session cookie; serve the page with `Cache-Control: no-store`; atomically read and delete the nonce when the POST arrives
mwg:verify-email-ownership:2.blocker: Storing the expected nonce directly in a client cookie lets an attacker replay the cookie and token together (quote: "never store the expected `nonce` value directly inside a client cookie where an attacker could replay both the cookie and token")
mwg:verify-email-ownership:2.outcome: Each nonce is single-use, back/forward navigation won't reuse a consumed nonce, and intercepted tokens can't be replayed (official claim)
mwg:verify-email-ownership:2.story: The token is bound to the nonce; if the nonce also lives on the client, one captured pair works again and again. Keep the nonce on the server and delete it on use, and replay becomes pointless.
mwg:verify-email-ownership:2.support: Same as mwg:verify-email-ownership; recorded as Limited

mwg:verify-email-ownership:3.title: Verify tokens only on the server with established libraries, and check DNS delegation before trusting `iss`
mwg:verify-email-ownership:3.action: Parse `EVT~KB-JWT` with SD-JWT/JOSE libraries such as `@sd-jwt/core` and `jose`; before trusting `iss`, check the `_email-verification.<domain>` DNS TXT delegation and that `.well-known/email-verification` reports the same issuer; verify the EVT signature and the KB-JWT nonce, audience, freshness, and algorithm allowlist
mwg:verify-email-ownership:3.blocker: Verifying tokens in client-side JavaScript can be trivially bypassed or forged and gives the relying party no trust guarantee (quote: "client-side checks can be trivially bypassed or forged and provide zero trust guarantee to the relying party.")
mwg:verify-email-ownership:3.outcome: The email step is skipped only after the whole cryptographic chain verifies on the server; any failure falls back to a traditional verification email (official claim)
